utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Mr. Nick Bano who has joined my team and is a pro bono legal assistant for the stand-by team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Just one housekeeping matter. Yesterday, a document was admitted as P4498, the Supreme Command minutes. That had actually previously been admitted as P3149, so it does not actually need a new number. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellency. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good morning to you, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind both you and myself that we should pause between question and answer and answer and question for interpretation. In this case the Defence is allowed pose leading questions and I would like to show you a number of very useful documents. So I would appreciate it if, whenever you can, you answer with a yes or no. And of course, as always, you're free to expand if you feel that you have to say something more. Can we agree on this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 15682 from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for it to come up I will tell you what my intention is. It is my intention to show you documents and to show you that directive 4, whatever its contents, had no negative consequences for the civilians on the ground. The only negative consequences were for the army, for the military. Now, do you recall this analysis. It is entitled "Realisation of planned tasks from directives numbers 4 and 5" from 15 September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now see page 4 in the Serbian version and page 6 in the English. It should read 4. Perhaps in e-court it's the next page. Thank you. In the middle of this page approximately, it says: "The enemy with its front end ..."

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "... with its front end of the defence, the enemy took up the dominant elevations which were difficult to capture and they provided a good view for the enemy. They're organising and opening a surprise side fire and opening artillery fire on our citizens and towns." And then on the next page - in English it's page 6: "In view of the fact that the enemy -- that we were more numerous and had larger forces, the enemy had a very dense line." So is this a reference to the enemy's personnel?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is consistent with what you knew about it at the time, they were very thickly deployed and they must have had a lot of losses, and of course it was also very difficult for us to actually get to those elevations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to add something here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the density of the enemy positions was increased by the Muslims by using civilians. On the 18th of September, 1992, Milici was attacked from Srebrenica. In this attack, very few soldiers took part who were armed, but there were some 20.000, as far as Colonel Simic and I could assess on that day, the 18th of September, 1992, there was civilians who had pots and pans, drums, and they made a lot of noise. There was a racket. There was a lot of noise and this was psychological pressure on the population of Milici as well as the VRS which was defending Milici. It was defended by the 1st Birac Brigade and commanded by Svetozar Andric. So this is correct, that the density of the enemy lines and the deployment of personnel on the enemy lines was very dense, but I just have to say that that was strengthened and reinforced by civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to what you know as a professional soldier, would that be a violation of the Geneva Conventions; in other words, exposing civilians to an enemy fire, to our fire?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this was not the only instance. In many front lines, on many front lines, they did that. For instance, in Sarajevo the 1st Muslim Corps numbered 50.000 to 70.000 men at all times. They were deployed in combat formation over some 250 square kilometres, in other words, along that ellipsis that was controlled by the Muslims, which was 22 kilometres long and 17 wide. In other words, this area was the area of deployment of this anti-air combat corps, and I believe that was the greatest density in any battle-field in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We will have occasion to look at some excerpts from your book, so we will be able to discuss that then. Now could we see page 16 in e-court now. Let us see what the outcome of this clash was. General, do you agree that these losses that we suffered, 214 dead, 321 seriously wounded, 557 lightly injured - we had over a thousand casualties - do you agree that this could not be accomplished had it been an attack on civilians? It would only be so if the attack was against a very well equipped and armed military force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the English page reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English that will be page 24, paragraph 1. I believe we have it on the screens already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just scroll this down a bit, or rather, I would like to see the heading because I can't see from this text whose document this is, or at least if I could be shown the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's the same document we've seen before, the command of --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Then I understand. As far as I can recall, you asked me whether these losses, losses of this type, would be possible if an attack was launched against civilians or whether, rather, it would be possible in the case where an attack was against the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's what I wanted to know. Are these very large losses, losses that can only be inflicted by a military force, not by civilians?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Losses of this scale cannot be inflicted by unarmed civilians. They're only possible in the context of an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the last page in both versions. In English that's 34 and then over to 35 and in Serbian that's the very last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at the last paragraph, the sanitisation or restoration of the battle-field. The "assanation," the clearing up of the front was performed with tremendous assistance from the Sokolac team with our own forces and the identification of the dead and those who were disinterred from the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The accused is reading too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the interpreters. I thought that they had the text before them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, first of all, could you tell us, sir, could you confirm that the clearing up of the battle-field was an obligation that was regulated by law which entailed the removal of carcasses and dead bodies after any incident or any combat, in other words, a restoration of the battle-field?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I would like to explain what this acronym, ZMPM, means. That is the institute --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was another criticism of me. I didn't really know what that meant. Now, the second thing is: Is it correct that when we liberated Podrinje we discovered a number of smaller and larger mass graves where Muslims had interred the Serbs that they had killed in the previous year, in other words, from April 1992 through April 1993. And that those were people from those 150 or so villages that had been torched, and that was the main reason why this was no longer bearable. It could not be tolerated anymore.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We attended the disinterment, or rather, the burial of these disinterred bodies in 1993 in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that General Morillon also attended some of these burials in other locations?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do remember that General Morillon went to Cerska because we were accused of having committed a massacre there, and when he returned from Cerska, Morillon publicly said that there had been no massacre and no killings in Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we move to 1995, I will get back to this, whether there was a similar situation then. Now let me ask you this: Is it correct that we found on that occasion massacred, mutilated bodies. They were in body parts and we saw, we were exposed, to this horrible suffering that the Serbs had gone through. There was even an 18-year -- an 11-year-old boy's body there who had returned to get his dog.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the bodies that we disinterred in Kamenica. We found several bodies at a time that were bound together with barbed wire and probably tied to what must have been a haystack. And then they were set on fire and that's how they died, that's how they ended. And I can't really say that they were buried. They were just dumped into the ground as they had burnt. And I have to remind you that at that time you returned from Geneva and you told me that I should ask the pathologist, Dr. Stankovic, to pay attention to the sexual organs. On the next day I went to the burial site, and when I said this to the pathologist he got furious. He said, You know, I'm an expert and I know what my job is. But I do understand what you were aiming at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But is it correct that it was frequently the case that the genitals were massacred and that there were instances ranging from circumcision to castration?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that, but when I was in Kamenica the pathologist told me that they found, they had found, there were instances where they found genitals of men in the mouths of the killed persons. And what you warned me about, that they should pay attention to the genitals - and that's probably what you also had in mind - was to make sure, or rather, to establish whether there were any circumcised men among the bodies; in other words, that there weren't any Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 9085 from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is another order, can you see, very urgent, an order to implement or launch Operation Fist, which was also grounded on this directive number 4. Would you please take a look at the first paragraph where the reasons are given for launching this offensive. It says: "Muslim forces on 8th January 1993 carried out an offensive in the area of the south slope of the Glogova Planina, Kravica village, Glogova village and are trying to extend operations towards Bratunac, and then by linking up forces on the wider area of Srebrenica, Cerska, and Kamenica, direct operation towards Kalesija and Tuzla. "During the above combat operations, the Muslims destroyed nine Serbian villages in a cruel and vicious manner, killing 49 men, women and children and wounding more than 50 people." Do you remember this massacre around Christmas time in 1993, the Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there is a typographical error in the document. The document was registered on the 10th of January, 1993, and the first paragraph starts with the words "the Muslim forces on the 8th of August" -- oh, sorry, 8 through 8. It's a mistake. It should be between the 7th and 8th of January carried out, and so on and so forth. I remember the massacre in Kravica where exactly 49 persons were killed, civilians. That was done exactly on Christmas day, Orthodox Christmas day, the 7th of January, 1993. Otherwise, in all of their campaigns Muslims chose to act on Orthodox Christian holidays, Easter day, Christmas day, St. Peter's Day. They probably thought that we would be relaxed and unfortunately they were right often. The massacre in Kravica, as far as I realised later - I did a great deal of study on this - was carried out by civilians more than soldiers. It was villagers against villagers, Muslim villagers against Serb villagers. As a matter of fact, there is another version that some of them had been visiting the Serbs on Christmas Eve, and when returning home they killed entire families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your document. You probably recognise it. Do you agree that in number 3 you say: "Taking advantage of the peace initiative of the Army of Republika Srpska at the time of the Geneva Conference, the Muslim forces are trying to take as much territory as possible within the former BiH and to inflict losses on the Serb people so that they would have the most favourable negotiating positions in Geneva."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the question, General: This position of yours from paragraph 3, was it confirmed in practice, and along with this reason, did you see for yourself that during conferences Muslims made the situation in the theatre of war even worse with a view to sabotaging the conferences that were being held?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was my position throughout the war, so I don't see whether I was the person who wrote this document, or rather, signed this document. However, the fact remains that that is my position. When these peace conferences on Bosnia and Herzegovina were underway and also the previous conference on the former Yugoslavia, either within the country or abroad, whenever the Muslims did not like something at these negotiations they found a way of stopping negotiations by way of carrying out combat or turning the whole situation against you, against the Serb delegation. An example of that is Vase Miskin Crni Street. I'm still convinced that Markale 1 was a situation like that. I'm not sufficiently certain with regard to Markale 2 because I wasn't there. Whenever things went downhill for them at these negotiations or if you would offer something that would be favourable to the international community, the Muslims wanted the negotiations to stop in order to have the war continued. You can ask me about specific events, the ones that I mentioned. I can explain all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. If there's enough time we'll deal with that too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at the last page so that the General can see who drafted this for him and so he can see his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this Milenko Lazic who worked with you? Do you agree that this is your document?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document. It was drafted by the late Colonel Milenko Lazic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5350, could we have that, please. 1D5350.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please, at the same time when they were committing massacres and constant attacks, you are ordering to have convoys allowed to pass. And look at this, on the 27th of February, and you say in the first paragraph, in relation to UNHCR convoys transporting humanitarian aid to Muslims in the areas of Tuzla, Gorazde, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Cerska for which approval was also granted by the president of the republic, I hereby order. And then in paragraph 2, you say: "Once the convoy has been checked (inspected) it need not be checked again along its route, but our patrols should provide security for it as it passes through our zone." And 3 it says: "Continue providing the usual inspection of the control, which should be carried out by persons trained to do it who will be extremely professional and civilised in the performance of their job." General, do you agree that there are no consequences whatsoever that would affect the civilian population, no consequence of directive 4 or of their attacks against us. The civilian population should be cared for as if they are our own. They are allowed to receive food convoys as well.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every time such documents were sent to subordinate unit, I had to invoke your position because if I did not do that, as I did up here - that is to say, for which approval was also granted by the president of Republika Srpska - I was criticised from the grass roots, from the subordinate units. I was criticised. They said that I was not feeding Serbs, that I was feeding Muslims, and I always had to say, How come this happened? So if they really minded this, let them be angry at you rather than at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let us see that sometimes they were partly right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5349, could we have that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the 19th of February, 1993, that is to say just before that convoy. Please focus on Kamenica, and it says that they got ahold of some report from Srebrenica, and it says I had to withdraw from the Sase mine and they took that. What they showed on TV is not correct, Chetnik propaganda. Our fighters who fled after the attack on Rudnik, I hope you will return them here. In five days Bratunac will be ours. Let us just have food here, and these guys will take care of the rest. So do we agree that your subordinates were partly right, and did you notice that invariably after convoys the attacks became far more fierce than they had been before the convoys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English translation is not attached -- actually, the Serbian version is also duplicated attached as English translation. Could we see the English translation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is an English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's now uploaded.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is Jasenica. I don't think this is it. This is Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is wrong again, yes, it's 1994. Original is dated as 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the previous document was the right one, the previous one in English. 1D5349.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you move on to the next document, coming back to this document later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you. We're going to tender it then as well. Let me just see whether I had put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you agree that this is proof that they can hardly wait for this food to arrive and for them to continue fighting? And do you agree that always after convoys their attacks became far more fierce?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, this document was not produced by the command of the Drina Corps, as the heading says. It is an intercept and this is what the Muslim side was saying. Now, I don't know where this was intercepted, was it from Tuzla or wherever. So this shows what the Muslims had heard about us, that we were preparing for the northern front near Zvornik, then also what Naser Oric agrees with, what he disagrees with. I mean, when we go back to this document -- well, what I'm trying to say is that this document does not speak about the situation in the Army of Republika Srpska and its intentions. These are the results of intercepts of Muslim radio communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this explanation, General. On the basis of what they're saying, can we not the see that they're just waiting for food to arrive and then they would attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I told you to move on because we don't have English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sorry. I apologise. 1D5352, could we have a look at that now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this order? Further operations after the 9th of April, 1993, and you say that a strong attack should be launched towards Srebrenica straight away. And in paragraph 2, you say: "In the attack on Srebrenica, I categorically prohibit any mortar or artillery targeting of the town of Srebrenica itself." Was this the result of all of these attacks of theirs, when one simply had to attack?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is mine. I say that on the basis of the number and my signature. I cannot exactly recall the situation when I issued this document, but I stand by what I wrote and signed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, this order when directive 4 was in force, does it give due consideration to civilians or is it aggressive towards civilians?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does give due consideration to civilians. Do recall all military operations that I was carrying out between my forces and between the enemy forces there were never any civilians, Muslims, Serbs, or Croats. The area between us was always cleared, I had always cleared it, regardless of whether we were defending ourselves or attacking. If the Muslims tried to do something as they did in Operation Sword near Medjedja, the village of Medjedja, when they tried to insert a group of civilians between us, then I simply went around that village and I did the same thing another time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the other incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the other village. The first one was Medjedja, and the other one?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdzici at the foot of Mount Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. And when the population is evacuated, which is also based on law, that means that they should not return after the fighting is over?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never evacuated the Muslim population. I said that I went around them and I evacuated the Serb population before the fighting. I did that, for example, in Grahovo in 1994, in December, late in December. I evacuated the civilian population, the Serb population. I evacuated Glamoc on the 28th of July, 1995, Glamoc did not fall because of the force of Croat arms. I evacuated the population and I withdrew about 1500 civilians and the entire Glamoc brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. However, in the question, line 13, or rather, line 14, there is a mistake. My question was: That does not mean that the evacuated population cannot return later. Here it says that they could not return. So these civilians were not moved with the intention of never having them return. They are just supposed to be removed from the area if there is fighting going on, and that is what the law says; right? Regardless of whether these were Serbs or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember now which document I could cite here as an illustration, but mainly the population, the civilian population, would be evacuated but they would return or could return after the combat. For instance, I did that on Grmec in 1994. General Dudakovic had expelled Serbs from the villages of the foot of Mount Grmec, torched them, destroyed them, and when the Serb forces launched a counter-attack, the civilian population was moving behind me into these ruins. And if you recall, I asked for the state commission to come to Grmec to assist me because I was unable to feed properly even my own soldiers, let alone the civilians. And then you sent Velibor Ostojic and Radoslav Brdjanin on this mission, these two ministers from the government who spent the night with me there, and unfortunately then just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted as Defence Exhibit D2141. General, this was addressed not only to the Drina Corps but also to various brigades of Drina Corps directly. Is it usual practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not standard or usual practice. This only referred to documents that were marked like this one, very urgent. In other words, you wouldn't wait for a regular procedure. And it was for the commander of the -- so we wouldn't have to wait for the commander of the Drina Corps to study, analyse this, and so on. But it would rather immediately mean that the -- that the instance that was to implement the order would immediately and that would probably sometimes be one step removed as subordinate -- would immediately proceed and act. In other words, this document required immediate action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D5353, please. 1D5353.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is another one of your documents, General. Now, in the midst of this operation - and apparently we do not have a translation yet, but this deals with figures for the most part so we can wait for the translation. But do you agree that in this midst of this operation you had no restrictions vis-a-vis the civilian population there, the Muslim civilian population, and that regardless of what was stated in the order you were allowed to -- allow humanitarian aid for civilians to get through, both for Muslims and Serbs. So could you just tell us about this. This is -- this refers to the Serbs in Visegrad, Foca; Muslims in Zvornik and Tuzla; the 13th for -- and the 17th for the Muslims in Srebrenica and Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just scroll it down a bit so the General can see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you don't have to scroll it down. I see that the Chief of Staff has signed this document. I just need a bit of time to look at it. Yes, this is my document and you can see that on a daily basis I allowed or ordered convoys to be allowed through, convoys for Serbs but also in every one of these items I also allow convoys for Muslims to get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just pull this up a bit and look at the handwritten part where it is added: Forward this to the Zvornik, Bratunac, 1st Birac Brigade, Visegrad Brigade and the 2nd Motorised Romanija Brigade. Is that what it is? Somebody forwarded this immediately, this order of yours; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is probably the Drina Command Corps that forwarded this onward immediately. Probably they didn't have time to re-type it and then send it as their own order, so they just forwarded this document to the Zvornik Brigade, Pandurevic; Bratunac Brigade; the Birac Brigade; and the 2nd Romanija Brigade; Visegrad Brigade; and the 2nd Romanija Brigade which was under the command of Radislav Krstic, now General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are -- my microphone is not working. Yes. I think it's working. Mr. Robinson, shall I make a finding of violation of court order every time he uses untranslated documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I don't know that you've made an order that we have to have translated documents, but we try our best and sometimes it's because he comes up with the idea at the last minute to use the document and other times it's because of simply -- our resources are such that we can't get them to translation in time. But we do our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's very difficult to follow if the document hasn't been translated. Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding, Excellency, but we asked for translation of over 200 documents over a month ago and probably the translation unit was just swamped with them. It was documents that related to this particular witness. Now could we briefly pull up D43, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, General, that these massacres and the nature of a civil war where villages fight against other villages and civilians fight civilians, you mentioned that after the entrance into Srebrenica one could expect uncontrolled fury. Now, do you recall that this document of mine which was produced after I talked to you, it was ordered that all combat should cease, that there should be no entering Srebrenica, that the weapons should be surrendered, and fighters should be treated as civilians, and no investigations into war crimes should be undertaken until the situation calmed down a bit. Do you recall that, the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it very well. This order was drafted when you and I discussed the possibility of establishing enclaves in Eastern Bosnia, and that was the first time that I heard of those enclaves and I was happy because I thought that if the security areas became -- came into being, as required by the UN documents, then I would gain something from it, that there would be one-third of forces that would be blocked, whereas the rest of the forces could be used on the battle-field. However, that's not how it transpired. This order was probably the result of that conversation that you and I had on that day, that morning. But, Mr. Karadzic, I would also have to remind you of all the troubles that I had before it was possible to draft an order of this nature. I will remind you that sometime in late January 1993 I mentioned to you that you would have to give some consideration to the issue of Srebrenica and what to do with it next. And on the 5th of March, 1993, when I entered Konjevic Polje, we had already taken Cerska and Kamenica without any fighting thanks to Philippe Morillon. And when I entered there, you remember the acronym KP, Communist Party, but, in fact, it stood for Konjevic Polje. You then called me - I think you were in Geneva or London or somewhere with General Mladic - and I told you then, President Karadzic, you will have to decide what to do with Srebrenica. Srebrenica has become a military and political problem and not a target -- not a military objective. And you said then, Stop. Mladic was with you in the room and I could overhear him saying, behind you probably, no stopping, just move into Srebrenica. And then I asked you to talk to him and decide by the next morning what you wanted me to do because one of you was a supreme commander and the other one was the commander of the army. So I could end up in court. Now, you did not call back, so I called you sometime between 9.00 and 10.00 in the morning, the next morning. You had no decision yet, and I decided to stop; not because of your order or Mladic's order, but I learned from Morillon that there was some 64.000 refugees in Srebrenica. The mass grave in Kamenica had been -- had just been discovered before that. I had ten brigades around Srebrenica, and there was not a single fighter in that brigade. I believe I mentioned that this army was predominantly of police type, from the area where combat was conducted. So there was not a single fighter who hadn't had or who didn't have in Kamenica a friend or a relative or a brother. So I feared that if the VRS entered Srebrenica, I feared that there would be a massacre in retaliation as revenge. On the other hand, I was afraid of my own losses, because even though most of these people were civilians, I knew that Oric had withdrawn some 12.000 of his men into Srebrenica. So I assessed that if I were to move into Srebrenica I would lose -- I would have losses of some 3.000 to 3.500 soldiers. And that is why, Mr. President, I stopped then. Now, on the line where the Serb forces stopped, that is where the border of the future protection zone was to be, and this was in light of this order of yours that I've said all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see P4704, please, to show what the position was on other enclaves. P4074, please. Well, very well, we -- it's not necessary. We can move on. Could we have page -- or rather, could we have 1D5354. We'll just continue along the same line we were going before. 1D5354. That document has already been admitted and it shows that the civilians were free to do whatever they chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this agreement on the demilitarisation of the protected zones, in this particular case, Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And the protected area for Srebrenica and that agreement was signed by the commanders of the warring parties, Ratko Mladic and Sefer Halilovic, and the guarantees were provided by General Morillon, the UNPROFOR commander. This was done on the 8th of May, 1993. And as for Zepa, an agreement of the same type was signed on the 18th of May in 1993. As for Gorazde, I cannot recall the date, but it followed soon after that. After these agreements by the commanders of the warring parties, which was in keeping with the Geneva Conventions, the Security Council of the United Nations - and I can't recall the Resolution number which proclaimed this - declared protected areas unilaterally without any agreement of the commanders of the warring parties of Tuzla, Sarajevo, and Bihac. Now, first of all, the way it was -- they were declared guaranteed that they would be unsuccessful in advance. These -- this was sure in advance because the Sarajevo, Bihac, and Tuzla areas were not delineated, either on the ground or on any maps. And this was not binding on the Muslims in Sarajevo and Bihac to disarm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will move on to that probably, but is it correct that this document talks about the requirement that there would be disarming in the next 72 hours, the demilitarisation of Srebrenica will be completed within 72 hours, and that they would have to hand over all mines, explosives, ammunition, and so on. And that the responsibility for the pacification and demilitarisation of Srebrenica was to be with the UNPROFOR forces? And this was explicitly stated and it was not ambiguous in any sense in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can see the next page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: " ...remain in the town. UNPROFOR is responsible for the demilitarisation process." [Interpretation] So here it says UNPROFOR is responsible for the demilitarisation process. So is this completely unambiguous and had it been implemented you would have -- there would have been no casualties and you would have had more forces?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, please, when you put questions to me don't then continue to explain them because then I don't know when I can start answering your question. But the answer to that question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted? Could we have a look at the last page, General Milovanovic sent this, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5355, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this order of yours dated the 18th of April, in which you ordered that you should halt at the lines reached, opening fire is prohibited, bringing in new forces is prohibited in the wide Srebrenica sector. Do you remember this? Not a single bullet should be fired. After the period of time mentioned, not a single bullet or projectile should be fired from a weapon of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the result of your order dated the 16th of April that we were analysing just a while ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it says again that -- it repeats everything stated in that order. It will be on the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 6 you speak about demilitarisation. In item 5 you talk about the evacuation of the wounded, about the organisation of UNPROFOR, two doctors from the VRS. Yes, that's the page. Item 5 mentions evacuation; item 6 mentions demilitarisation. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the implementation of the agreement reached by the commanders of the warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page in the Serbian version and I think it's also the next page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that here you are ordering the manner in which mines will be cleared and the terrain will be cleared. In item 6 the same words are used that we used in my order, the civilian population has complete freedom to decide whether to remain in Srebrenica or to leave. No party may hinder the freedom of movement of civilians. Muslim combatants are to be treated as civilians after being disarmed. General, is it quite clear here that whatever directive 4 says doesn't concern civilians and the civilians didn't suffer any consequences as the result of directive 4?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2144.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D5361, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's another order of yours, General. 1D5361. This is an order of yours after the signed agreement dated the 8th of May, 1993, the cessation of combat, and you refer to the agreement on the basis of the agreement between Mladic and Halilovic. In the presence of General Morillon you say, and you're issuing this order on the same day, you mention a total cease-fire. That's item 1. Item 3, the total demilitarisation of the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde sectors. And here you planned for the weapons to be surrendered to UNPROFOR, not to us. Can we have a look at the next page. Item 5 you are prohibiting entry for representatives of the VRS into the Zepa, Gorazde sector and apart from the representatives of the above-mentioned members of the commission. And under 7: "Members of the so-called Army of BiH, once the weapons are handed over, are to be treated like other civilians and freedom of movement is to be ensured for all so if they wish they can leave the said regions or remain there." General, this very favourable for both sides and especially for the Muslim civilians? They are not to be treated as POWs but as civilians. When they stop fighting they become civilians.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let me say something about the conditions, the circumstances, under which this order was created. The results of the agreement were known to me. I found out about them over the phone. In the course of these negotiations these two commanders from the warring sides and General Morillon were involved in these negotiations and Morillon wasn't convinced he wanted to persuade the Muslims of something. He said that General Mladic didn't have a centralised command in the VRS. It meant that we weren't an army that had been organised in a contemporary manner, in a modern manner. He asked General Mladic to open fire on a certain target, mostly in Podrinje. Mladic called me and asked me how long it would take me to open fire on some feature, I can't remember which feature was concerned. I said I can do so immediately. However, he confounded me when he said, Fire. I conveyed the order to the Drina Corps command and fire was opened in two or three minutes' time. A few minutes later Mladic called again and he said, This person still doesn't trust me. Open fire on this target. Artillery fire has numbers, so I can't remember exactly what it was. We opened fire again and I asked him, Boss, how long am I to continue using our ammunition? But finally he understood the situation and realised that we had a centralised command over the VRS. So that was proof of the manner in which Morillon entered these negotiations, but the idea to create a safe havens was his idea. His idea was also to have the population in Srebrenica transferred -- the Muslim population from Srebrenica was to be transferred to Tuzla on the 14th of March; and the Serbian population from Tuzla, 17.500 could go to Podrinje. I told him that that was ethnic cleansing, regardless of the fact that we were -- or rather, that he was trying to save the civilian population. He said, That's my problem. Tolimir and I negotiated with him. We had to make a note of this. I think Tolimir sent a report to you about the matter, or rather, to the Supreme Command. The evacuation of the civilian population from Srebrenica commenced. But priority was given to the wounded, and the evacuation continued until 12.500 people were taken out of Srebrenica and then it stopped. I asked him, General, not a single Serbian was taken out. He said, Your Serbians don't want to leave Tuzla. They are concerned about their flats. Why did you stop with the evacuation of these people? He said, I've obtained my objective. But later I understood that he had taken out members of Naser Oric's army, about 12.500 men. There were some civilians amongst them, mothers, sisters, children, but on the whole he saved Naser Oric's army from being destroyed in central Podrinje. So much about that so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, whenever possible I'll try to obtain yes or no answers. Do you remember that the Muslim population, especially those who weren't originally from Srebrenica but were from the surrounding places, continually strove to go to Tuzla. And our assessment was that it would be easier for their army to fight if they had fewer civilians?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no because Alija Izetbegovic, even earlier we spoke about this yesterday, issued various proclamations and prohibitions on leaving Sarajevo and Srebrenica. He prohibited the civilian population from leaving. The Muslim army did not want to be left without the civilian population. They used the civilians so that they could have the civilian population in the vicinity of military targets. So I could not agree with that. Our desire was to remove the civilians so they didn't hinder the armies. I mentioned the villages of Medjedja and Hamdzici yesterday but we weren't successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was general so it wasn't precise. Did the civilians have certain desires, and Izetbegovic, did he have different desires?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a different kettle of fish. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, could we now see 65 ter 4219 to see where directive 4 comes from, or rather, where -- why it is that there's certain imprecisions in directive 4. While waiting for it, do you remember the crisis in Vecici village, in Kotor Varos? Two weeks before the directive, directive 4, do you remember that there was an ultimatum from the Muslims to have their civilians allowed to leave Vecici and for the troops to remain? And there was a misunderstanding, a dispute, between me, Mladic, and Talic. Mladic accepted my agreement; Talic executed the idea, but there were reservations. Have a look at this. Do you remember this matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is all your comment. It has no probative value at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I didn't intend to make any comments, but I wanted to summarise this so that the General didn't have to spend too much time familiarising himself with the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Once you've read through it, let us know, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the end Mladic agreed to let the women and children leave, but Talic thought that the troops should also hand over their weapons and should leave with the population. The troops should not remain behind in our rear.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Talic in this document made the same request I made in directive number 4, and that was that the troops shouldn't remain behind after the civilians had left because Talic was the commander in the field and he wasn't going to leave troops in his rear. That would be illogical. But I can see that the man carried out General Mladic's order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this translation is a finalised version. It didn't translate the heading. Is this your Defence team translation, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's from the OTP. But "explanation" means "explanation." So the title is somewhat incomplete in graphical terms, so it would be better to have it translated again, to have a literal translation. The Serbian version is quite clear and unambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls, is this from other case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, precisely. It's a Defence translation from the Krajisnik case, which is why it's -- appears in a different format. I'm trying to see if we have one ourselves, but it doesn't appear that we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification until confirmed by the CLSS, or are you happy to admit it as it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This document I do not object to its admission with the translation that we have, and we can just check it if necessary to provide an updated one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D2146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, let me not call up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll mark it for identification or we'll admit it in full, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we want -- we want to have an official translation, a more precise one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, let me not call up documents now because you're familiar with them anyway. Do you agree that in our language there is a substantive difference between these two sentences, that the army should leave with the people; and the second one that the people should leave with the army? Could you please explain what the first variant means, for the army to leave with the people in the spirit of our language; and what the other variant means, that the people would leave with the army.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wish of the opposing side or of the enemy is that every time the people withdraw, the army of that people should withdraw too. That means that the army should leave with the people. On the other hand, there can be another wish, for the people to leave with the army. However, that wish is not exhibited by the commanders of the warring parties. That wish is exhibited by the people. Yesterday I talked about the tradition of China, France, and Serbia, that people follow the army or go with the army, either in front of it or behind it. Here's an evident example. In October 1994, the people of Grmec were moving in front of their army, that is to say they were withdrawing. A month later, they were moving behind their army. So as the army was advancing, the people were following. There is a linguistic difference: With the army or with the people; however, the meaning is the same. It means that the army is leaving certain areas. Is the army the first one to leave and then the people follow, or the other way around? The only difference is that the enemy wants the army to leave the area with the people, and we know which people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Bearing in mind what happened two weeks before directive 4 and Vecici, do you agree that when one says the army should leave with the people, it means that the people were leaving anyway and they should take the army along as well, as opposed to a different situation when the army would be leading the people.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to help the interpreters. Oh, I see they have made a remark of sorts. So if it says that the army leaves with the people rather than the people with the army, is the first case that the people lead the army and the other case is the army leads the people?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case of Vecici, General Talic wanted the army to leave with the people, or rather, for the people to lead the army out of Vecici. That is how I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that also reflected in directive 4? It's not that the army should leave and cleanse the people, but rather, since the people were leaving anyway then the army should leave too, and the analogy follows Vecici?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although when I wrote that directive I did not have Vecici in mind. This was the strategy of the Army of Republika Srpska. When there is no local population, then that population's army is not there either. We simply wanted to have a clear situation in a particular area. However, I have to warn you. All three armies in Bosnia-Herzegovina, except for the regular army of Croatia and later on the NATO Alliance, the armies of the three warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina were armies of a militia type. They were linked to a particular territory, although we manoeuvred with our units from Krajina for Sarajevo or from Herzegovina to that Visoka Krajina of yours. Nevertheless, these armies were attached to territories, to municipalities. When a population moved, there was no guarantee for me that my army would stay in Drvar a month after the population of Drvar left. The Muslims had the same situation. When the people were no longer in a particular area, then the army - unless it's expelled by the enemy - will withdraw on its own anyway. They simply cannot keep on staying there. These are peoples' armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now call up the directive now. Do you agree that the directive says that they should unconditionally surrender weapons, and in Zivanovic's order it says that they should unconditionally surrender? Is that a significant difference? The directive says that weapons should be surrendered, whereas he misquoted it by saying that they should surrender unconditionally?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a vast difference. In the directive it says "surrender of weapons." And later on you saw in the orders that implemented directive number 4, it said specifically for Srebrenica soldiers who surrender weapons will be considered civilians and will be treated as civilians, whereas Zivanovic wrote compulsory surrender of fighters. Now, these are two different things all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. With the agreement of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, can I ask you to take a look at a Prosecution exhibit during the break and another 65 ter document so that we would put questions faster and more easily, if everybody agrees. Could you please use part of your break to read these documents that you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Nicholls? If it is items are known to you. Would you like to take a look?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. In principle, no objection, Your Honour, unless of course the witness wants to, you know, really take a break during the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3040, 4245 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it to you, General Milovanovic. We'll have a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may take a look at these documents, perhaps I have them in the waiting room, just so I know which documents are involved. I do not mind taking a look at them during the break. I just need to see what the documents are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, have you had a look at these two documents during the break?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I compared them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we first call up P3040 just to establish one thing. Paragraph 2, "Tasks of the Drina Corps." Let's take a look at that. Next page, yes. "Tasks of the Drina Corps." Do we agree, General, that this was a copy-paste situation in relation to directive 7, these general tasks?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page. Paragraph 4, that is usually the decision itself. Do we agree, General, that in this paragraph all the way until the end of the document - so this has to do with the decision of the commander of the Drina Corps - there is no trace whatsoever of any kind of controversial sentence or controversial intention. What was pasted in the introductory part is not repeated.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a difference and there should not be one. Specifically, it has to do with Srebrenica and Zepa in case UNPROFOR leaves these two enclaves. There is a reference to Operation Jadar. In the first part I did not notice that remark, what to do with Srebrenica and Zepa if UNPROFOR leaves them. Srebrenica and Zepa are mentioned within the context of other built-up areas with a tendency of blocking them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the second paragraph here. In co-ordination with the forces of the SRK and the Herzegovina Corps as Star 95 is being carried out, liberate Serb areas in the enclave of Gorazde and reduce it to a protected area of 3 kilometres from the centre of town. And in case UNPROFOR leaves Srebrenica and Zepa, Operation Jadar should be carried out and that is when Muslim forces should be crushed and destroyed in these enclaves, and Podrinje should be definitely liberated. Do we agree that this refers to Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now move on to this next document, 65 ter 4245. Do we agree, General, that this is a document of the Drina Corps that is based on directive 7/1, so eight days after directive 7/1 was issued by Mladic as an executive order. The commander of the Drina Corps issued this order for defence and active combat operations. That's it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This order of General Zivanovic was produced exactly 15 days after the first order that was based on your directive. However, this order, since it was of a more recent date, was supposed to annul the first order, Zivanovic's first order, because it has to do with the same problem, the same operation. However, Zivanovic did not do that. He did not mention at all that that previous order would no longer be in force. Secondly, in this order he only refers to two brigades, the Zvornik Brigade and the Bircanska Brigade and in the first one he gave tasks to all brigades of the corps. The tasks of these two brigades that he mentioned here match, to a degree, the tasks given in the first directive. However, he did not give any tasks to the other brigades here, at least he did not repeat them. So these two commanders cannot resolve in their orders the problem of neighbours and the organisation of co-ordination. Now that we're dealing with these two documents, towards the end it says that the documents were drafted by the same person, the same author, Colonel Lazic. However, they were not registered under the same number. If we look at the heading, it is the number of the operations administration, I think in one of them it is /3, and now the second one I haven't got it here with me, something was added in pen, /4, so it was not registered in the same person's documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha. May I remind you of the following: The 20th of March, 04277-2, that is the number, and this more recent one is 03277-3, and it's right, this was added in pen, 277-2, that was added. So this one should annul the previous one; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is based on the principles of control and command, that the order with the most recent date, unless otherwise stated somewhere in the text, automatically annuls the previous one. It would have been smarter for Zivanovic to have written this up as an amendment to an order or a correction or whatever. So what he wanted to do here was to satisfy the Supreme Command but the Main Staff as well, because you see he's doing this 15 days later. Mr. President, at the time obviously the Drina Corps command got itself confused as well as its units. Now, if you look at the brigades that were given these tasks in the second order, they are slightly different if compared to the first order. Now, as for neighbour brigades, they know what the original order was, but they don't know what the second order was. So the commanders were not able to co-ordinate action with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I didn't follow when the witness discussed what was added by pen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the earlier ones, the protocol number was entered by hand -- well, perhaps we can pull it up, that's P3040. The protocol number was added by hand. I guess they didn't know when it was. Now, the other document was typed, typed up, but there was the same number but then what follows is -3. So the protocol number was entered by hand in pencil, and that can be done if they did not know the protocol number at the time when they wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'd like to hear from the witness. Is that what you said, Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's exactly what I said. On the last page of the document, we can see that the same person drafted both documents; however, the same person did not register them as their own number. The first one was registered by Milenko Lazic, who had this mark -2, whereas the other one had -4 which means that it wasn't the same person. Now, whether it was the same person or not who registered them, it doesn't really matter; what does matter is that the signature of General Zivanovic was there, the signatory of both these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, this will be admitted as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, General, you are right, there is a Latin proverb saying lex specialis derogates the lex generalis. Now, there is another example where we can see how an even later document superseded these, and I believe we have a better copy, that's 65 ter 19577. 65 ter 1977. It has already been admitted. There is a P number for this document; however, this copy is clearer, it's more legible. Yes, this is the document. Now, please take a look at it. Can we agree that the protocol number was entered by hand here as well, and it is dated the 2nd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're trying to prove to me that this is indeed possible. Well, it is possible. Now, when a document is very urgent, it would be sent immediately to the teleprinter operator, and once the teleprinter operator has sent it to the end user, then it would be returned to the administration to enter this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor showed you this document with the intent of pointing out that directive 7 was implemented or how it was implemented and how it had an effect on this executive order. Now I would like to show you page 5 in Serbian, I believe, and in English that would be page 7. The -- this paragraph was not shown to you. Could we please have 65 ter 1977, not the P number, because the reason we asked for the 65 ter version was that this copy is actually smudged, the P copy.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What paragraph do you want me to look at?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's just wait for the more legible copy, the clearer copy. Here we have it. Now, please take a look at the following. The security organs will send to the subordinate commands for their information the regime of security in combat areas and there should be heightened security while preparations are made for an attack.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, my apologies. But before that, security organs and military police organs shall establish the areas where prisoners of war and the war booty will be concentrated. In this, in the treatment of the prisoners of war and the civilians, you are to abide by the Geneva Conventions in every respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we discuss this, can we not upload the English translation of P4421 so that we can follow. 1977 does not accompany the English translation. Mr. Nicholls, you agree that 1977 is just a copy of the same document which does not have the handwriting part?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, it doesn't have the handwriting. I'm taking a look. I was trying to see exactly where 1977 was sent to, to see that it is exactly the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but the first page looked the same. Very well, let's --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 7 in English. Page 7 in English. Page 7, paragraph 1. Before the "Camouflage "section. Yes, here where it says "Security."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here it appears crossed out, but in fact it should be underlined, it shouldn't be crossed out, the portion that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the Serbian version. Does it say here: "Security organs and military police will indicate the sectors for gathering and securing prisoners of war and war booty," and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So instead of underlining this section, this portion, it is crossed out here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I see the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we see the original of P4421, i.e., the 65 ter number 15583.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could I see the first page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1977, yes, before we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In B/C/S 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you want to see the English page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I did, I saw it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you. Page -- what's the page number of Mr. -- of B/C/S, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5. In Serbian it's 5 and in English that's 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, General, that somebody tried to underline this but he wasn't very precise and that the Geneva Conventions are not even underlined?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot really be the judge of whether this is underlined or crossed out. The way I see it, it's crossed out. However, the previous copy you showed me on the screen didn't have this. But there was an imprecision not in the text but you've said it. You said the security organs and organs of the military police, whereas it should only read "security organs" and they would implement this through the military police because the military police is their instrument of action. Because should it remain as it is, it would mean that the military police also has the authority to issue orders, whereas they only can implement orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. General, could you read the handwritten part at the top of the page. We can -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The section where prisoners of war will be secured is in Pribicevac. The sector where the prisoners of war and war booty shall be deployed is in Pribicevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, General, does it say that the security organs and those of military police shall stipulate this, and then by hand, on top, somebody added "the sector where prisoners of war and war booty will be deployed is in the Pribicevac sector"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct. This sector or this area was added by hand by the person who was responsible for deciding where that will be. However, this sentence is not principled. The sector where prisoners of war will be centralised as well as war booty and their security shall -- is normally something that is done by a logistics unit, the rear organs. And security organs, with the help of the military police, interrogate prisoners of war and perform a triage so that when it is determined that a prisoner of war had committed a war crime, that person would be separated and taken into custody and prosecuted. For those for whom it was established that they had not committed a war crime, they would be taken to a centre, a camp, where they would await an exchange or whatever. So the security of prisoners of war is something that is organised by logistics -- the logistics department, whereas the security organs and the military police only performed a triage. And of course they also tried to obtain as much information as possible on the situation or the status of enemy forces. However, a prisoner of war under the Geneva Conventions is not duty-bound -- is not obliged to answer to any questions other than what his name was, what his name is, what his rank is, what unit he belonged to, and the number of his military tag. Those are tags that are issued to all troops in case of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, after the sentence "Geneva Convention," I take it, whether it is an underline or a striking out, on the right side does it not say "nee," which I take it to mean "no"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's a question -- I asked you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my answer to that will be: Yes. The person who processed this document felt it necessary to exclude this obligation of the security organ. Now, why that person did that, probably because they thought that every officer would know what I mentioned just a moment ago, what are the questions that a prisoner of war must answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, I remember you rose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I've been jumping up and down. First of all, I object to the representation unless there is some foundation and basis made in the question this was underlining not strike-through and putting that to the witness. It is clearly -- I was going to try to make the same observation that Your Honour just did about writing no. It's clear it's a strike-through and different changes. Second, this is indeed a version of Krivaja 95. It's -- just to be clear, the version we were looking at before has the Drina Corps stamp on the end. This is the version received at the Bratunac Brigade, and that's the stamp at the end of this one, so it's the version received at the Bratunac Brigade that we have handwriting and strike-throughs on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can admit the clean version that was admitted in -- received by the Bratunac Brigade, if you wish, Mr. Karadzic, and continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Excellency. I just want to see through this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you agree that there was a clean version from the corps that was sent out from the corps, and someone in the field issued an order and said that these handwritten additions were added in the field? This wasn't done in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank the OTP for that intervention. I now know who underlined this and who crossed this out, and so on and so forth. It was the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. At the time it was Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic.
