When he examined this document, he immediately made notes for himself to see what should be done with regard to each item, and he drew the conclusion that the sector where these things would be gathered for his brigade would be in Pribicevac. He wrote this down immediately. He came to the conclusion that provisions for the work of subordinate commands with regard to interviewing witnesses were not necessary. He put "no" there. We know who sent the document. We know he didn't -- the person who sent the document didn't cross this out, but the person who received the document, who was to act on the document, made these markings. Having marked the document, this person already provided guide-lines for the operations officer who had to draft an order of his own, so that one could know what to -- what should be taken into consideration. So the operations officer wouldn't take this sentence into account in the order that he drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Can we agree that the person who issued the order and the brigade commander didn't tamper with the sentence that said: "When treating POWs and the civilians, make sure that you abide by the Geneva Conventions"?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, yes, because when this was crossed out the commander of the Bratunac Brigade assumed responsibility for deleting certain parts of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we take the date into consideration, the 2nd of July, and a fresh document replaces a new one, that's a principle, can we agree that regardless of what the previous documents state, in this case, in this document, it is stated that the Geneva Conventions have to be abided by and the person who issued the order and the brigade commander didn't believe it was necessary to delete this sentence or to amend it in any way?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm testifying here, or rather, I'm not testifying about the events that I saw, the events that I participated in. This is on the 2nd of July, and I don't know whether I was in a tent or on the Golja mountain. However, these comments I'm making are comments that I'm making as someone who is aware of the process of creating and distributing documents. I don't know what the brigade commander had in mind when he crossed this out. I don't know whether he thought that it wasn't necessary because everyone knew about this. I don't know whether he thought it wasn't necessary to carry out the corps commander's order. So he deleted this and assumed responsibility for this act. I can't answer this question precisely by saying yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, the sentence "on the conventions," is it something that is not in dispute for the person who issued the order and for the brigade commander. This is the part that wasn't crossed out. It has to do with action taken. Please have a look at the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this sentence is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the latest document -- well, this was the freshest or the latest document, and as such, this was the document that had force; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the document sent from the corps also be admitted, not just the one that was amended in the brigade, because the corps' intention was not to have these amendments made?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit the 65 ter number 1977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we need to translate it again. The translation should be the same, Mr. Nicholls, but only that the crossed-out part or underlined part will revive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We do have a translation, if I'm understanding, of the Bratunac Brigade-received order with the crossed out shown and the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The original one is 15583 has translation, yes. I'm talking about 1977, which does not have any handwriting part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that's correct. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Am I correct? I'll check with the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Another option for the Registrar is to add this document to the previous exhibit, P4421. I think that's more convenient in terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, with both translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's acceptable for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue -- yes, General, you have something to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. While you were conferring I had another, closer look at this document. The question as to whether this was crossed out or underlined -- well, with regard to that issue I would say that it has been crossed out because the commander personally undertook the obligation to indicate a sector, and he wrote this at the top. It's not the obligation of the security organ anymore, and this part down here was also crossed out, the commander confirmed this by making a note of "no." This hasn't -- this doesn't have to be included in the order. He probably thought that all the officers were familiar with the Geneva Conventions. So my conclusion is that it hasn't been underlined, because if it had been underlined, it would have been emphasised in some way. It was crossed out so that others did not have to think about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at this 1D15349, and we have the translation. 1D5349. We've had a look at it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you are right, our service was listening on to what Oric and his associates were saying and in the lower part where it says Kamenica it says: Drive out in five days' time. I hope you will return those who fled. Drive them out in five days' time. Bratunac will be ours. Food should come in and these young men from the group will complete the task. Do we agree that it is clear here that they are waiting for a convoy and after that they will be ready to go into combat? This is 1993. We've called up this document now. You provided authorisation for the convoy. There was a convoy before this and after this.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted or has it been given a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 65 ter 16354.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you wrote a book at the Prosecution's suggestion, if I'm correct, because you provided information about the war and this information was appropriate for the purposes of writing a book. I think we have a translation and we could see the translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we have translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I'm sure that The Hague Tribunal has a translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at 1D5159. We have the pages we are interested in translated there and we have nothing against the translation of the entire book. Could we see the last page. The first and last cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you are the person in this photograph, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should be me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Do we agree that if we don't include the introduction, the page -- the book has about a hundred pages and you stand by this book and by the information contained in this book?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by everything, apart from the critique and the biography because I didn't write that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this please be admitted, with the exception of the additional texts that weren't written by General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the point of admitting a book without putting a single question about the content? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we discussed this, and this is the problem: There's so much information that this witness has that we're going to have to call him back in our Defence case if we don't -- given if we don't find some other way to present his information to the Chamber in the time that's allotted to us. So we were hoping that by submitting this book we could later on refer to the items in the book in lieu of his oral testimony, and that was the idea we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we consider, can I be hearing the views of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We absolutely object, Your Honour. This is about 127 scanned pages. I think this is some kind of 92 ter process they're trying to do. We don't have a translation of the entire book. The -- there isn't yet any crisis in time for the Defence presentation of their case, and the perfect remedy -- this doesn't come under 90(H) or getting evidence favourable to you through questioning the witness. If there is a huge amount of favourable information which they wish to call from this witness, they ought to call him in their Defence. And I would probably want to cross-examine on some of the material in this book, which I have not read and can't read at the moment. So I strenuously object to the entire document coming in, and it would be against the practice we've had of referring to pages of this type of material, which is in essence they're offering it as an enormous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber absolutely agrees with the views of Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Karadzic, if you so wish, you go through the important parts. And as long as you stick to the relevant part, the Chamber never limited your time for cross-examination. We'll not admit this in such a hasty manner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. I was just afraid that I wouldn't have enough time, but if we have enough time we'll go through certain things without calling General Milovanovic again. Could we see 23620.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you write a text "my meetings with the president of the republic and the supreme commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic"? Did you do this during the war? And was this text created for the needs of this Tribunal, or rather, for the needs you felt you had as a witness who came to testify here? We have a translation of this document and we are looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did write this immediately after you'd been brought to The Hague because I knew that I would be involved as a witness for the Defence or for the Prosecution, it was all the same to me. I wrote this down as a sort of aide-memoire so that I could refresh my memory. I read through this at least 15 times. I read through it a few days ago and last night, too. I provided it to your Defence team about -- well, I think at the end of 2009 or at the beginning of 2010. I thought that you would provide a copy to the Prosecution; however, when I was being proofed by the Prosecution on the 31st of January and on the 1st and 2nd of February, I saw that they didn't have a copy. So I provided them with one. So here it says how I obtained the information, on what basis I obtained such information, and I also made a note of my conclusion. Since the main source of information was, well, relying on my memory, it was therefore necessary to consider this material to be fairly precise or backed up by arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Could we have a look at the next version, the Serbian version, and it's also the next page in the English version. Do we agree where you say again in the evening on the 14th of May this first meeting, when I told you that Serbs were trying to avoid war but we could not sacrifice political freedom. So you gave a rather accurate description of our contacts here; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I just correct something in relation to a problem we came across yesterday. Yesterday we discussed an order dated the 26th of May, 1992, and what it says there is the following: On the basis of talks held between the Main Staff and the members of the Presidency - and then this follows - it says -- actually, on the basis of the talks between the Main Staff and the authorities of Republika Srpska on the 26th of June. I think -- it's not that I think. That's a typo in that text. It should have said dated the 16th of June, and the document was issued on the 26th -- I beg your pardon, on the 26th of May. So this document from the 26th of May is actually a product of this meeting of ours that was held on the 16th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Since this was created for the purposes of testifying here - and as far as I know the Prosecution does not oppose having this document admitted - I am tendering the document. If we have enough time left, we can go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This document seems to be different. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2149, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, now I'd like to move on to the topic of the relationship between the supreme commander and the Main Staff. So I'm going to remind you of an interview with a Prosecutor that you conducted on the 2nd of July, 2007; that is 65 ter 22556 on page 130. The Prosecutor asked you about what happened on the 12th of May when the Army of Republika Srpska was established. And you say that a decision was made -- actually, do you remember. It says here I was not appointed a member at this Assembly, it was Mladic who was appointed. The Assembly appointed Mladic, and after that he had the freedom of establishing his own team; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mark Harmon was the Prosecutor I talked to in Banja Luka on the 2nd and 3rd of July, 1997 -- sorry, 2007. And perhaps my statement was somewhat modified through translation, but this is what I stated. At the Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, a decision was passed on the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska. It's not that the army was established as such. Secondly, the Assembly appointed Ratko Mladic commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and authorised him to propose appointees for his assistant commanders, commanders of corps, Chiefs of Staff of corps, so all people who would hold the position of general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, now I'm going to try to summarise as much as possible so that we can have as many yes or no answers as possible. Did you confirm in that interview that Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do we not have English on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was my question, if I could just have the English page reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English is noted as "translation." That may be the problem. I can see from my personal computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm fairly certain, at least, that the English would be the original version. It should be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What page in English, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's 130. I didn't want to tender the document because this is viva voce testimony. I just wanted to get answers as to whether what had been said was correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But we need to follow. Is this the correct page, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this seems to be the beginning. It should be page 130. In Serbian it's 130. Just a moment, please, I don't know what page it is in English. Actually, it's not even the right page in Serbian. No, the page is not right in Serbian or in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While it's being found - I don't know what page it is - can I have your position, General. Did you say then that Mladic was appointed by the Assembly at the time and that he was authorised to set up his own team, and that that was the reason why attempts made by the Supreme Command to have Mladic replaced were not successful because it was only the Assembly that could have him dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could not replace Mladic, but you could make a proposal to that effect to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Further on, do you remember -- actually, is that not fresh in your memory, the night before the Assembly when you agreed what should be done by this army, whether it would be an offensive or a defensive one. Can you tell us what it was that was discussed on the 11th of May, on the eve of this Assembly meeting? What was it that you, founders of the army, discussed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, General. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm -- I'd -- I'm not suggesting that there's any misrepresentation, but I do object to conducting the cross-examination in terms of "you said this" and "further on you said that," if I have no way of following. So maybe he can put - as Mr. Robinson has suggested to him before - just put the question rather than saying "you said this" if we're not able to follow along and -- because if it's represented that "you said this," then I want to be able to check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. I was about to say to the accused the same thing. Just put your question. It's quicker, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, can you -- do you remember the question, General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember the question. The question was roughly what it was that we discussed that night between the 11th and 12th of May, 1992. It was explained in detail very precisely in my book. On one particular page there are eight points where I said what it was that was discussed exactly. Should I repeat that from memory, if I can?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether it is correct that on the 11th in the evening you agreed about a few important things, that it would be an army of defence, that it would be a depoliticised army? Can you tell us what the essence was that you reached at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That evening we did not adopt the actual tasks; rather, we adopted some conclusions on the basis of certain principles as to what we would do the following day once the Assembly passes its decision. Our first conclusion was, or one of our first decisions was that the future Army of Republika Srpska would be based on the already existing of the Army of the Territorial Defence of a militia type, and that is what the leadership of Republika Srpska started after the 4th of April; that is to say, between the 4th and the 20th of April. That was the establishment of those brigades of the Territorial Defence in the municipalities that were on the outskirts. That was the first mainstay of the army. The second mainstay of the army would be the remains of the JNA, both in terms of manpower and equipment. Thirdly, we would go for the existing paramilitaries in order to include them in the future Army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Further on, the system of supplying the army would be based on municipal organs of government, that is to say those who established a brigade would support it until we find a more favourable solution. Further on, we had the intention of excluding Crisis Staffs from the system of command and control; over the army, that is. Crisis Staffs would stay on and carry out their duties that had to do with taking care of citizens in situations of imminent threat of war. And we also envisaged imposing a state of war as such so they could do everything except command units. I've already mentioned paramilitaries. They were supposed to be built into the system of command of the Army of Republika Srpska or they should be expelled or destroyed. As far as morale is concerned, the morale of the army, all of a sudden we were moving on to a system -- well, I cannot say that we were moving from a communist, but say a socialist system of governing society, and from that we were moving on to a purely Serb army. So there is no brotherhood in unity. We will be fighting our hitherto brothers. So then we went to the sources of morale; that is to say the traditions of the Serb army, faith, enlightenment of members of the military as regards the objectives of our struggle. Also, we built in a segment that had to do with commanders and officers giving, or rather, setting an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you agree then that the Geneva Conventions should be observed and, in a way, you expressed faith in one another or loyalty; rather, if one of you is replaced, then the rest would follow?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that conclusion about observing international humanitarian law follows what I already explained, that is to say the building of combat morale, and that is one of these principles of ours. Could you please repeat the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The second part of the question has to do with the following: Is it correct that in a way you pledged loyalty to one another? In case one of you is replaced, then all the others would resign?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I omitted an important thing in relation to these principles of ours, and that is that we were building an army of defence. At strategic level it was of defensive character and in terms of operations and tactics it would be offensive. That is very important as far as the nature of the army is concerned. As for this question, this last one, that is not part of the principles, that is not part of the system of command and control. Rather, the 12 of us pledged ourselves to one another, that we would go on operating as a team. And if one of us is dismissed for political reasons, that is to say if somebody or a political party that is in power does not like us, then we would all leave the positions we currently held. We would go back into the trenches with the troops. We made the corps commands aware of that when the Main Staff was first assembled, and that was the 26th of May I think -- no -- yes, the 26th of May. We made them aware of that at the proposal of General Talic, and all corps commands accepted that. They said that they would do the same thing. And that was one of the explanations I gave to you. When you tried to dismiss General Mladic, I said to you that we had undertaken this obligation amongst ourselves and that you would no longer have any commanding personnel if that were to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I remember. Is it correct that on several occasions I asked you to take over the command, that is to say the Main Staff, and on each and every occasion you gave this same answer. So it wasn't only once, it was several times?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, twice it was orally. On the 6th of August, 1993, in Pale; and on the 3rd of August, 1995, in Drvar at my command post. The third time it was in written form by way of an order on re-naming the Main Staff into a General Staff and my appointment as head of this General Staff, and you assigned Mladic to a position of special advisor to the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about this error being incorporated into the Law on the Army, did you -- do you agree that because of that error we had a two-headed army and armed forces, instead of having the Main Staff become the staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and I stand by it as I sit here. However, command and control of the army during the war was not two-headed, as it were, and that is mainly thanks to the Main Staff. We remained under your personal command and you know very well that no one from the Supreme Command could issue orders to the Main Staff other than you. So you were that link between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now please just elicit short answers. Can we agree that this carefulness of yours came from the fact that a party that was not a socialist party had won in the elections, that there was a change not only in the regime but also the entire political system, and that there was danger that there might follow a clash between the new regime and the old army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The result of that cautiousness was something quite different. We -- when speaking about the army that still existed and it was mentioned yesterday, some 85.000 to 90.000 armed men, we found, in fact, some kind of Chetnik strategy of fighting in their structures. That would be camping as a method, and then if somebody attacked a Serbian town or place then they would just rise and go. And by the time they reached there, the place would have been destroyed and it would have been too late. As for the officers of the Army of Republika Srpska, a large number of officers at the lower level of command and control were in favour of the Partizan strategy of warfare. I believe that was the result of the previous 50 years where we were taught and trained in this tradition, and we assessed that neither strategy was viable for us. The Chetnik strategy could not -- we could not win with; and as for the Partizan strategy, that was not viable because of the territory. But also because of constitutional provisions, the provisions of the constitution of Republika Srpska. The constitution of Republika Srpska obliges the citizens of Republika Srpska to defend the well-defined territories of Republika Srpska and to defend and protect the population lest the genocide of 1941 through 1945 repeat itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered one of my intended questions. Is it correct that the leadership set two objectives for the army. The first one was to prevent a potential new genocide and the second was to defend the people and the territories until a political solution was found. Yes or no? We can deal with this easily.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that at the time of the Vance-Owen Plan, the tensions were high, and do you agree in principle that this tension between the civilian and military structures did not -- arose from different approaches to what the new state system should be like, so it was really of doctrinary nature?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned crimes as a possible reason for these differences in approaches; however, I would like to correct you. There was the Vance-Owen Plan, the Stoltenberg Plan, the Contact Group Plan, so I'm not sure which one you're referring to exactly. I believe that's the one that you signed in Athens. That was not the reason, Mr. Karadzic, for our differences. The reason was that we based ourselves on these two provisions of the constitution. The army did not want to allow the crumbling of Republika Srpska, its disintegration, or division into these 10 or 11 cantons. So we opted for armed struggle in order to maintain an integral Republika Srpska; you opted for diplomacy. Up until early 1995, the army provided for you, if you recall our telephone conversations, my first sentence would usually be, Mr. President, you can take the high ground because we have an advantage. Or, if not, we would say, You would need assistance from -- we would need assistance from diplomacy. So this was where our differences were. The army was in charge of the war, whereas you were in charge of diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in one of the documents that we've admitted I read that you actually had a grudge -- held a grudge against me because I said at some point that our army was too combative - is that correct? - this was said in the context of the different proposals for peace resolution that were coming in the context of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe you said that at the Supreme Command session of the -- of August 6. This was an expanded session when we reached Bjelasnica and Igman because then the negotiations were already underway on our withdrawal, and then I said, Well, how can the Supreme Commander not want to have a combative army? Now, that was the first thing but then I also objected to your statement that we did not wish to defeat the Muslims and I even –- objected to something that the Patriarch Pavle, when addressing the Serb people, said. He said, We should not hate the enemy. We build combat morale on the hatred toward the enemy. Now, all of a sudden you are urging us not to defeat this enemy; and on the other hand, the patriarch was calling on us not to hate the Muslims. So that was contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Subsequently there -- it was said that you were the initiator of establishing new contacts with the political leadership that had reached it's slow point at that time?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th of August, 1995, that's when it came about. Now, you know the Assembly session where Mitsotakis and Milosevic attended, and the Assembly declined to accept your signature. Milosevic was putting that in the context of push back but win the war, and somehow with that position of his, he seemed to take the upper hand at that session of the Assembly. After that, Milosevic and perhaps the Greeks, I'm not sure if they had part in that sent Perisic, because he understood that the army was the one that was against the implementation of the Contact Group Plan, so he sent the Chief of the General Staff Perisic to us, to the Main Staff, so that he could talk reason to us. Now, we spent the whole afternoon discussing this, looking for a way out. Now, the civilian leaderships of Republika Srpska and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia too were not functioning too well. And in search of a way out, I said that we in Republika Srpska first have to re-establish our ties with the civilian authorities of Republika Srpska, that we had to establish co-operation, that after that Assembly session we even stopped exchanging opinions with each other. And it was not expected that General Mladic would be so offended, and he asked me then, What was it that you said? And I said, Well, we should re-establish the links with our political leadership, and only then can we put pressure on them for them to renew the contacts with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Then he said, could you repeat that one more time so I can write it down. And then I realised what it was all about. He was actually against that. There were other people there. Some of them were rumbling and I wasn't sure if they were actually opposing what I said or what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you remember, General, that I asked you to withdraw the army from Igman and Bjelasnica, that you said that then you had to deal with this hot potato, but that then I asked of you to withdraw from Igman and Bjelasnica but in the least painful way; in other words, to hand it over to UNPROFOR, not to the Muslim army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, and even as I sit here when I think of those days, the 12th, 13th, and 14th of August, 1995, I still feel uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was another reason why -- which explained this tension between us - correct? - because the civilian leadership - or me specifically - in view of my obligations arising from the negotiations, I frequently actually was an obstacle or presented an obstacle to the army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way; however, I never said that you obstructed the army. But I did say on a number of occasions - and I will reiterate it - that you made some moves without previously consulting the army. Let me remind you of the problem between the two of us that had to do with pulling back the air force and the anti-aircraft defence. This started on the 24th of August, 1992, and was at its peak in October 1992, and then it lingered all the way through the adoption of the Resolution 816 of the Security Council on the no-fly zone over Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 31st of March, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But is it true that your logic, the military logic, was not to withdraw, whereas my position was that we should withdraw because that arose from the negotiations. And is that what caused these tensions between us when talking about Bjelasnica and Igman?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean between you and me or between you and Mladic or do you mean between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff or me and Mladic. You heard from both of us from Geneva; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. One was pulling one way, wanted me to stop; and the other was pulling the other way and demanding that I not cede territory; in other words, you were asking me to withdraw and Mladic was asking me not to cede the territory to the Muslims. Or five months earlier, as we discussed this in Srebrenica, you staid Stop, and Mladic said, Move into Srebrenica. To be honest, it wasn't fair on either one of your parts. And the two of you were together there. Now, the other case, Igman and Bjelasnica, I had strict orders from you to pull back. And until the breakdown in communications - if you recall I was in a vehicle when we were talking - I had this idea how to actually carry this out, how do I withdraw the army but not cede territory? So when I said this to General Hayes and I said my supreme commander wants me to withdraw the army but not cede territory to the enemy. And then he said, well -- he probably already had a clear idea in his mind. He said, General, I will help you. You withdraw your army and I will take positions of your forward positions and I prevent the Muslims from taking control of that territory. Had he not been a man, I would probably have given him a kiss then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, do you remember that I told you that I was under pressure to replace Mladic and I wanted to move him to the political leadership, but you said not only because of that covenant that you had between you, that that was not possible because he could -- not only because of that covenant but also because only the Assembly could actually dismiss him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we have a date or a time-frame for this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As of 6th August 1993, do you remember that I told you then that there were pressures, and then after that, on another occasion, I told you --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was on the 3rd of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in 1993 that was August 6th, and this was in the context of Bjelasnica and Igman?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then on one occasion I said that you would take over the army and I said in May. Now, the 6th of August, 1993, before we go on break, can you just briefly describe what it was about. What did I ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, but you have to stop adding things on because I'm looking at the cursor and I don't know when I can go on. Well, there were other reasons and I presented them to you. Do you remember that I asked you then who would be my boss? Because I thought that that was your final decision. And you said that you would be my boss; in other words, that I would take over command of the army. I said that I would not do that and I mentioned the reasons, the loyalty that we pledged to one another and so on. Then I said that Mladic was able and capable to command the army. I told you, Mr. Karadzic, that Mladic's authority in the army and amongst the population is something that I wouldn't be able to accomplish through the end of the war. Whenever Mladic showed up anywhere and said, Let's go, nobody would question it, they would just follow him, whereas I as -- or a corps commander appeared somewhere, we would always have to justify what we were asking. As you can see from all those documents, there is always some kind of explanation in the preamble, explaining why we are ordering so and so, whereas in Mladic's documents there was no such thing. And I also said that I'm more useful as the chief of the Main Staff in the VRS than as a commander of that army because the chief of the Main Staff is the position which actually unifies everything from supplies through combat use, and this is then presented to the commander. I felt that I would be more useful in that position than if I were to be the commander of that army. So those were my reasons. Now, the reasons that I had on the 3rd of August, 1995, were somewhat simpler and shorter. One of them was - and I told both you and Krajisnik of this - I said, Which fool would take over command of an army while it was withdrawing throughout the front and which would be followed by loss of territory?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, may I just ask or say, rather, that the Defence would not mind to have a shorter break or, if possible, to extend our work today past 3.00 p.m. today because I would like to show as many documents as I can to this witness because he's a very valuable witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that you want to conclude your cross-examination during today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd rather not, Your Excellency, but I'm not sure how much time I still have. I'd rather have the General come back on Monday, if that's possible. Because the number of documents that he had seen and decisions, relevant decisions, that he had to do with are very relevant and would be very helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just asking, General Milovanovic, for planning purposes, is it a possibility for you to stay till Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would rather stay than have to come back on another occasion sometime later, which is what happened in one instance earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll take a break now and then we'll see how it evolves. We'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.33 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, is it correct that you considered Mladic to be a fairly reasonable person when it came to military issues and you could influence him, but in political terms it was difficult for politicians to deal with him and to have a dialogue with him? He was inflexible, in political terms.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic is fully fledged military individual. That concerns all aspects of the military. He has a sort of natural or so-called natural intelligence that assists him in drawing conclusions. As to how he dealt with you, the politicians, well, you're in a better place to know about that than I am. But given what I could see when I participated in your conversations, it's true that he was inflexible. He would never budge an inch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that on one occasion I told you that I would present you with a fait accompli in front of the journalists and I would say that I'd handed the army over to you, that you would be the commander of the Main Staff. And you said that you would deny this and that this is not something that could be done without there being an Assembly decision?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was on the 6th of August, 1993, when you and I went to give statements to 100 or 150 journalists. That's about how many there were in front of the Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that in December 1993 I was angry because I never knew where Mladic was and I would have to ask you about his whereabouts, if you knew about them. And then I asked you to come and see me privately to have a conversation in Pale, and there I also suggested that you take over the army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 10th of December, 1993. On that occasion you suggested that I -- or rather, you didn't suggest that I take over the army. You said that it would be better if I were in command of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not really in the transcript, but is it true that I was a bit critical because I never knew where Mladic was, and therefore I said that you were a better soldier than your commander because you would say where you were, whereas in his case I didn't know his whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was after you had explained the reasons for calling me. You didn't want us to talk as the supreme commander and the Chief of Staff, but you wanted the conversation to be a private one, between two men, Karadzic and myself. I said that although you wanted this conversation to be a private one, I was obliged to inform General Mladic of the fact pursuant to the law. Then I said that General Mladic was in Belgrade, and you then said that I was a better soldier than Mladic because I would report to my commander, inform him of my whereabouts, but he didn't deem it necessary to tell you that he was leaving the battle-field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that after August 1994 sanctions were imposed upon us. The SRY imposed sanctions on us and officers no longer received their salaries. So given the dissatisfaction or not to say the revolt in the Eastern Bosnia Corps, you went along with me to speak to those officers?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia imposed sanctions on us on the 4th of August, 1994. On that occasion, the officers did not receive their salaries for the following three months. However, in May 1993 after the difficulties concerning the Vance-Owen Plan there was a five-month period. I was with you to calm down those officers who were in revolt -- well, I can't say in revolt because they didn't use their weapons, but they were dissatisfied and they wanted to speak to you and General Mladic. General Mladic sent me to speak to them and he said that you probably wouldn't have anything against it. That was his justification. You wouldn't have anything against me being there. And certainly he was afraid of whom he should support. He had to support you, the supreme commander, or rather, he had to justify your actions, but he couldn't let down the officers over whom he had command. And we were down there together. You know how the meeting ended. No one was satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Chamber what my reaction was. Could these officers have told me everything to my face and did everything end in a democratic and positive way?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The officers told you all sorts of things. First of all, someone spoke about the reasons for calling you there. Colonel Slobodan Jelesic, the deputy commander, the assistant commander of General Simic for morale, spoke about the reasons for calling you there. And then you gave the floor to the participants at the meeting. Everything would say all sorts of things. The best way to depict the atmosphere there is for me to mention Momcilo Krajisnik's speech. He was there with you, or rather, with us and he said the following: Radovan, aren't we fortunate to have such officers? We will certainly be victorious. Given that they can tell you the sort of things that they have told you, then you can imagine the sort of things that they could do to the enemy. And you used those words of Krajisnik so that the meeting would end successfully for you and for me. You accepted all their comments, all their objections, and you promised them that the state would not forget about its officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't angry with them or with Mladic for not being there; isn't that correct? I had nothing against you being there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You were not angry, but I was angry with the officers on that occasion because they applauded Krajisnik's speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in June or May or the beginning of June, perhaps, I issued an order that concerned retiring the Generals Gvero, Djukic and Tolimir and Colonel Beara. I didn't succeed in doing that and later I didn't have any contact with them. It was as if they had retired or been sent into retirement. That was in 1995, May or June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was in May 1995. I personally considered that to be a manner of sanctioning the officers because of the way they conducted themselves at the Sanski Assembly on the 15th of April, 1995. I think that they were sent into retirement. I think that General Gvero, General Djukic, and General Beara and Tolimir were sent into retirement. But there were no other interventions up until 1996 to ensure that that order was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I no longer considered them to be our officers. I no longer asked them to submit reports to me, nor did I have any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say because I really don't know whether you had contact with them or not. They didn't complain to me. I know that they continued to communicate with me and Mladic, so I can't confirm that nor can I deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was clear to you, was it not, that in the Main Staff that the daily reports that were sent to the supreme commander were read by my advisors, and is it true that you were critical of my advisors? You didn't consider them to be sufficiently capable or sufficiently educated to provide me with correct advice, adequate advice?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your position was that when it came to military matters I was quite subject to -- well, I could be easily influenced. I wasn't a professional and as someone who was in favour of Republika Srpska I didn't take my interests into account. And according to you, many of my assistants influenced me and tried to pursue their own interests through me.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was your position that my advisors should be sufficiently capable to distinguish what was important from what wasn't important and they should provide the president with important information, information that had been selected according to relevant criteria, and they should also put forward certain proposals, certain solutions?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I came to that conclusion at our first meeting on the 16th of May, 1992, when Colonel Tacic was attacked. First this was fabricated; and secondly, it wasn't the most important piece of information provided to you by the Main Staff. There were far more serious problems; for example, liberating captured officers and soldiers and family members in Sarajevo barracks. There was the problem of raising the blockade of those barracks and there was the problem of the JNA's withdrawal. That was the 16th of May and the dead-line for withdrawal was the 19th of May. Instead of discussing that issue, we discussed the fact that some colonel had allegedly taken 12 tanks from Vlasenica to Serbia, which was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But apparently it was correct that the whole rocket brigade had been taken out by him, so we didn't have as much equipment, as many weapons that we could use to defend ourselves from NATO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which rocket brigade you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think there was a rocket brigade in Romanija before the war and he was responsible for it and he took it to Serbia, to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I've heard about that. I know that we kept surface-to-surface rocket brigade from the JNA of the Luna type. We kept the 155th Rocket Brigade, the anti-aircraft defence 155th Rocket Brigade. There was the independent rocket regiment somewhere in Romanija or Sokoca [phoen] area. This is the first time I've heard about this brigade that was taken there, and Tacic didn't have that establishment speciality that would have enabled him to be in command of a rocket brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that from the 1st of July up until about the 4th of August, I mainly communicated with you, and as a result I sent you, in fact, reports and I sent you my decisions. And as a result, other generals were a little suspicious about this. It was from the 1st of July until August 1995. Nevertheless, you had to report to Mladic about this and you had to carry out his orders. And in exceptional cases, you had to report to the second in command, your second superior.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that happened in the month of July up until the 6th -- the 4th of August, 1995, not all the time, though, if I understand you correctly. But it did happen a few times. However, whenever that happened I cautioned you or General Subotic, saying that the system of command was being duplicated. I never refused to carry out your order, but I would forward that order to General Mladic as my first reporting officer. And then I'd wait for his answer. Usually the wait would take about 24 hours. If I received an answer, then I carried things out the way he had wanted them to be carried out. If he responded to me, he mostly supported your orders. If I did not receive a response, then I acted on your order. The problem with that was doubling the time for carrying out the order, and that was the reason why I voiced my criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you had an objection because I was almost unnaturally peace loving as far as the Bosnian Croats were concerned, and this happened, although they attacked the Serbs if they were not at war with the Muslims, for example, in the Lasva river valley. And is it true that when the Muslims expelled them from the Lasva river valley, the Army of Republika Srpska took them in at Vlasic and acted as their host?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To this day I'm angry with the current president of the Republika Srpska because he plays along with the Croats way too much and then in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina they turned their backs on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show you something now, General. The Prosecution showed an example of where things developed rather smoothly in our communications and in the transmission of orders. Now I'd like to show that we had great difficulties in this respect too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the General please be shown 1D05438.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this additional order that had to do with the order not to bring into custody national deputies or members of the MUP and government, because that kind of thing had happened?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me - because I cannot see myself - is this a document from 1995 or 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this, but I do remember a document - that's why I asked whether it was 1995 or 1996 - because I remember that in the heading there is a reference number and then there is /96 and then underneath it says the 18 of September. Now, I really cannot see whether it is 1995 or 1996. If it is 1995, I do not remember the document. However, if it is 1996, you issued a similar order in 1996 after that mutual arrest. The civilian authorities were arresting generals, and General Mladic responded by arresting civilian authorities; however, the war was already over and it had to do with the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. This is an old Serbian habit. Once the war against the enemy is over, then it starts against the Serbs; right? Actually, you don't have to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted? So it's the Main Staff and this is being sent to the 1st Krajina Corps, although I think it should have been sent to the 2nd Krajina Corps. And now I'm going to show you this other document. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, he didn't know anything about it, I thought. He knew about an event in 1996, if I followed, but he said he didn't -- if this is 1995, I don't remember the document, and then spoke about a different event in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, do you know -- you said -- actually, you said that the war was over, practically over, September 1995, when the 2nd Krajina Corps, in contravention of my orders, ordered the mobilisation of the top people from the MUP, the business community, et cetera. And then I ordered that that should not be done and I added this to that order. Do you remember all of this? This was sent to the Main Staff in September.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not recall, although at the time I was in the area of the 2nd Krajina Corps, that is, September, and there is combat against the Croatian Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have a look at 1D05440.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember now? For example, the 2nd Krajina Corps is ordering the mobilisation of the leaders of the business community here, and that upset me because that means that the economy grinds to a halt and it was hard for us to feed the army anyway.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was signed by the late General Tomanic, and I do not recall it, although I was in his command. However, this is the end of September, it's the 29th, and that previous order of yours was issued somewhat earlier. I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we then just look at 1D03904 from the 2nd of October. Actually, I'm interested in the principle involved, General. The 2nd Krajina Corps, did it have to act in accordance with my order or was there some misunderstanding there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not sure how it relates to your case. While complaining about shortage of time, I would like you to concentrate on more critical issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to show, Excellency, that there were quite a few misunderstandings and there was a lot of friction, too. For example, the order that I called up a moment ago, that this other order that was here should be annulled, and look at this: On the 4th General Mladic is responding to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For example, do you remember this, General?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember this at all, although I was in the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, do you remember Mladic's letter sent to me dated the 4th of October, where he says we analysed the order and so on and so forth, order issued to the 2nd Krajina Corps, and on the basis of these facts we concluded that the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps acted in accordance with the order issued by the superior command and that this order would be carried out in subordinate units. So I'm just trying to indicate what the principle is and that was not always easy. And can we have a look at 14324, that would be the 65 ter number. Please take a look at this. Do you agree that after all it was stated here that the 2nd Krajina Corps would act in accordance with General Mladic's orders and that I could not have my decision implemented?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this order because it did not have to do with the forward command post. It was sent directly to you from General Mladic, so -- I mean, quite simply, I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did General Mladic have to act in accordance with my orders?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have 1D05441 and then we are going to decide on how admissible this is later. So this is two days later that I'm answering General Mladic. Also, I concluded from his document that number 2, my order had not been carried out. Number 3, that in this way the authority of the government, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of the Interior, and so on, is being infringed upon. And can we move on to the next page now. Please take a look at this: I hereby order that the order changes in the order issued by the Main Staff ... be carried out straight away and that the provisions that apply to managers, et cetera, should be repealed. Do you agree that it was not easy to implement all of my decisions? For example, Milutinovic, Radio Krajina, many other things. It was simply not that easy to implement my decisions with regard to any of this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you, that it was hard for you. However, there are few things that I'm surprised at. You know what your attitude was towards General Tomanic, specifically. And I'm surprised that Tomanic did that, or rather, that he did something against your will. He carried out General Mladic's order. The man is dead now, but he was sitting on two chairs, if you will. Secondly, I'm surprised that the Main Staff, or rather, General Mladic rebelled against this order of yours when the Main Staff itself, as far as I know - let me work this out now - three, four times asked for you to intervene through the MUP so that the MUP would help us with the additional mobilisation of certain areas where the military police was insufficient, or to have the MUP help us in some operations. Quite simply, the author of these papers of Mladic's disregarded the fact that we had asked you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do not do this gladly, but I had to present this because the Prosecution wanted to present things as if they were moving along smoothly. And now I would like to have all of these documents admitted because they speak about the difficulties that were there, how difficult it was to be in charge of the state and the army in a principled way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Mr. Robinson could expand on the relevance, how it relates to the period relevant to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe the period relating to the indictment goes to November 1995, first of all, so I think we're well within that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's in that -- could I -- could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: If we look at the -- I'll have to call it up, but if we look at the indictment, the question of the -- how long the joint criminal enterprise lasted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but the crimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- committed after --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we certainly have Markale 2 on the 28th of August, 1995, that's -- at least we have that as a specific crime. But I think the -- and Mr. Tieger can speak to this more authoritatively than I can, but my understanding is that the indictment periods covers -- this is within the indictment period. If I could also say, to me this goes to the core of the case with respect to Srebrenica, the issues of effective control --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- ability --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just wonder if my friend can think about whether or not this should be in front of the witness. I don't know what he's about to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it can be in front of the witness, but you can stop me if I'm saying too much, but the issues that we're dealing with here deal with issues of effective control and the ability to prevent and punish the crimes in July of 1995, for starters. So it seems to me to be very relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just add something. This had been going on from 1993 onwards. The General spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you have examples 1993/1994 which the General is aware of, why don't you use it? I will consult my colleagues. Would you like to respond? But you do not challenge the authenticity of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just that they are late, as Your Honour points out. The -- and the witness did not know about this -- these alleged difficulties about mobilisation of businessmen in the western part of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just add two more things. Number one, I think he gave enough context to this dispute to admit the documents; and number two, I'm just reminded in -- was with the last witness the Prosecution was introducing documents from January and March of 1996. So I think it's not very fair to call something in September 1995 late, especially when the duty to punish exists after the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The 1996 documents, if they're the ones I'm thinking of, referred to cover-ups and events which occurred in the heart of the Srebrenica, what we consider, week of crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although the witness was not able to confirm the content of these documents, certainly it relates to a topic which he deals with, i.e., the relation between the military on the one hand and the civilian political authority on the other hand. And in that regard, the Chamber finds that it will be assisting us. Also, we note Mr. Robinson's submission, so we'll admit them all. So 1D5440 will be given Exhibit D2150, and 1D3904 will be 1D2151. Mladic's letter which is 14324 will be 1D2152, and the last, Mr. Karadzic's order, will be admitted as D2153.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can just assist, 1D05438, that is the additional order, will that also be assigned a number? Will it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2154, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, I would just now like to ask you briefly to see if we can agree. Do you remember that on the 30th of March there was the 14th Session of the Supreme Command - and you spoke about this during the examination-in-chief. Now, can we agree that after that time the exacerbated conditions had, as a consequence, a session in Sanski Most on the 15th of April, and this was when it culminated, when the developments culminated, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That session was held on the 31st of March, the 14th Session. That session did not affect negatively the relationship to the effect that they would come to a head at that session of the 15th of April in Sanski Most. In between there was another session of the Supreme Command in Banja Luka on the 13th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 13th of April you mean?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, the 13th of April in the evening. That is when these deteriorating relationship between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff came to a head. At that session we were supposed to discuss the final version of the expose of the Main Staff which the Main Staff was supposed to present to the Assembly. Simply, we were not heard. It was said - because you had received those materials earlier and they were probably -- they had probably been read by members of the Supreme Command. I believe that Krajisnik spoke for the Supreme Command and said that a document of this form cannot be presented to the Assembly. After this session of the 13th of April, we agreed that General Mladic would take the floor at the Assembly session and read out the expose, and that is what transpired. The Assembly session completed its work, irrespective of the events of the 15th and the 16th of April in Sanski Most. It ended amicably because neither you nor Mladic could afford to have the echos of this relationship become public. And then you met on the 16th or the 17th of April, the two of you, on Mount Vlasic. There is video footage showing the two of you inspecting the visit -- inspecting the soldiers on the front line. And after this session of the Assembly there were -- there was no reaction from either the Supreme Command or the Main Staff, other than --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch other than what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I understood that to be some sort of punishment meted out to the generals. But, Mr. Karadzic, I have to add something. After that Assembly session, the distrust between the supreme -- the Main Staff and the Supreme Command became very pronounced, and I could feel it in my position. Whenever any step was taken by anyone, the intentions were in contravention of the intentions of the other side. Well, first of all, the army did not get what it expected to get from that Assembly session, it didn't get anything. However, the Supreme Command and the Assembly did not heed or accept or acknowledge if anything at least the military assessments. Fourteen days later Operation Flash began and the Serbs lost Western Slavonia then, and the Army of Republika Srpska now had a direct enemy opposing it on the Una and Sava River. So this was in nobody's interest and neither side can be proud of what we did then on the 15th and 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see 1D3910.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can we agree, General, that irrespective of whether the suspicions were justified, that both sides were certain that they were correct in their suspicions. So the level of distrust was very high. And do you remember this letter that I wrote to the members of the Supreme Command and the members of the Main Staff. This was on the night after this session that Operation Flash began? Do you agree that the commander, the chief, the assistant commanders received this letter that I addressed to them on the 30th of April -- actually, my -- the date when I sent it was the 29th of April, but it was forwarded on the 30th of April. Do you recall that? If you wish and when you feel it's necessary, we can scroll to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not necessary to move on to the next page. I can remember this very well. Fourteen of us generals received this letter and not on the 30th of April. Rather, it had been brought by a courier. He was wearing a blue police uniform. He brought it to the Main Staff headquarters. Now, we were in the midst of an expanded session of the personnel administration. All corps commanders were present, and out of 14 generals who were present there, we were all accused - and that is how I read this letter and I said as much to you then. I still have it with me, it's there in the waiting room in my bag -- we were accused of preparing a coup d'etat. When we received it, we stopped with our work, we read the letter, and I was assigned by this entire group of people to get in touch with you and to ask you to have -- to convene a session of the Supreme Command at the headquarters of the Main Staff. At first you accepted this. This session was supposed to start at 4.00 p.m.. You were supposed to arrive there by 4.00 p.m. but you didn't, but you called me on the phone and you said that it was inappropriate for the Supreme Command to go to the Main Staff; rather, that we should go to Pale. I asked you whether we should also bring with us the corps commanders because there were a lot of them who were accused by this letter, and you agreed. We went to Pale. And on that day, that was the 1st of May, at 5.30 in the morning, Operation Flash was launched. And on the eve of that operation, or rather, on the 29th of April, when this letter was drafted, I had informed you and the Supreme Command of the Republic of Serbian Krajina that an imminent -- an attack was imminent in Western Slavonia on the 30th of April. That did not come to pass on the 30th of April. And then Milan Martic, the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and Celeketic, General Celeketic, sent a letter to you and to Mladic to the effect that I was again disturbing the people of Serbian Krajina, that there was no attack, that I was just trying to intimidate them and so on. And the conclusion was, like two or three years before that, that they did not wish to have any kind of co-operation with the main -- with the chief of the Main Staff. So when we had that session at Pale, it began with this issue. You ordered then that each one of the -- let's call them accused or individuals suspected of this, should prepare a statement, write a statement, and I said I wouldn't do it and that I would respond in writing. And I warned you then that it is impossible for an army to stage a coup d'etat in peace time. They can -- what they can do is they can mount a putsch which means that there would be a temporary take-over of power pending an Assembly session. Now, at this session the generals --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in your reply, didn't you, and this is for the record, that history will have a final say on this; it won't be me?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I can repeat that. I recall the words of General Krstic at that session. He was still the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. He said that for him General Mladic was an ideal military commander and that it would never occur to him to change his opinion about General Mladic based on this letter. I don't think it's necessary to repeat before this Tribunal what all happened at that session of the Supreme Command, whereas you should recall that I changed the course of this session of the Supreme Command because the supreme commander of the Republic of Serbian Krajina had sent a telegram that arrived in the midst of that session, informing you that the Republic of Serbian Krajina had engaged the enemy as planned earlier, which wasn't correct; that they had pulled out three brigades to the territory of Republika Srpska; that they had left one brigade in Pakrac and the surrounding area, as previously planned; and that they were preparing a counter-attack which was to be staged in two days, in other words, on the 3rd of May. And they were asking you to send them assistance in the form of an expert on counter-attacks. Not batting an eye, you told Mladic to send me there, and Mladic gladly accepted. Now, you know the outcome of that counter-attack and everything that surrounded it. We were in Banja Luka on the 3rd May, or rather, on the 4th May at 1.00 a.m. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, I would like it to be reflected that you said you would not give an answer to me because you count on history providing that answer, correct, when you refused to provide a written statement?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I said, as far as I can recall, the following: Mr. President, I refuse to write any written explanation. You will get an answer from history.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2155, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 15697 from the 65 ter list. I don't know whether there's a Serbian version, apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that General Mladic here forwarded a response to me from General Simic, the commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. This was in response to my request for him to state a position. Do you remember that he sent that letter. Could we have a look at the next page so that we can see his letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: There must be a Serbian version of this that we can get, otherwise we can print a copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.
