utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting, General, could I read out the beginning of item number 5 to you. It will be translated correctly for your benefit. It's on page number 3. Could we see page number 3, item number 5, so that the interpreters can see the passage I will be reading out. Item 5, and I'll read it out in English: [In English] "Your letter is also inspired by the mistrust of the professional officers of the Army of Republika Srpska nurtured by some representatives of the civilian authorities" --

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear the interpreters clearly because of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're hearing the Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you should read it out not so loudly, or the interpreter should be a little louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Not to interrupt. It's printing now. Maybe it would be simpler for Mr. Karadzic just to allow the witness to read the document or parts of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're waiting for the document I wonder if we might address, at this time, the schedule, how we're going to deal with the remainder of this witness's testimony and the other witnesses who are scheduled for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the end of the day it may depend upon how much longer the accused needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. If you prefer to discuss that at the end, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If we can discuss it now, how much longer do you need, Mr. Karadzic, to conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At least a day and a half or two days so that the Chamber can have the maximum benefit from this witness and so that the Chamber can gain an understanding of the entire war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in concrete terms, how many hours do you need?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Six to eight, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to say, Your Honour, to keep in mind an issue that was raised with the book. If -- there's a difference between cross-examination in the classical dealing with the evidence, which we led, and just putting in everything possible which could be useful through a witness pursuant to 90(H). If there is a lot of material that doesn't really go directly to my direct examination and the remedy may be to call the witness in their case, that's just something that I need to add, that 90(H) I don't think encompasses necessarily leading -- changing a Defence witness into a Prosecution witness and allowing just, you know, days and days of cross-examination which is really direct examination or should be direct examination. And the only other minor point is that at this stage I think I have at least half an hour, probably a little bit more, of re-direct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read through this. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First I wanted to ask you whether you agreed with the first sentence, item 5, where it says that from the beginning of the war there's a lack of trust fuelled by some of the civilian authorities. But do you agree that the entire letter is a manner in which one's own opinion is expounded in very strident terms?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before answering the question, General Simic was on his death-bed for a few days. I want to tell you about that. But as far as this letter is concerned, this isn't General Simic's opinion. It's the opinion of his collegium. He consulted his assistants. And if you want me to say whether I agree with it or not, I fully agree with what General Simic emphasised. And now the question is after the war I also found out that the -- according to the war, the army that had been depoliticised had several officers and even generals who were secret members of the party in power. They weren't allowed to be such members openly because they would have been driven out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you agree that in the party in power -- the party in power thought that all the generals were in the SK for Yugoslavia, the League of Communists, the movement for Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why we can't reveal our cards. Krajisnik and Kalinic had such -- Krajisnik and Kalinic had such opinions, and they would convey them to the municipal Crisis Staffs where they called the officers the red sort of group. We inherited Tito's system, they called us Milosevic's mercenaries, because Milosevic, or rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia paid us. And you're well aware of that fact, as am I. You know who these people were, and when they said these things they called us the red gang.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to scheduling issue. Mr. Tieger, when you said, was it yesterday or today, that Mr. Dean Manning is fixed, what did you mean in concrete terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I essentially meant, Mr. President, that not only Mr. Manning but both of the witnesses had to be completed by Tuesday. I had further discussions, managed to arrange for the possibility that Witness Djurdjevic could conclude his testimony on Wednesday, but certainly not any further than that. So that's what was meant by fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you said Mr. Djurdjevic could conclude on Wednesday, did you know that we are sitting in the afternoon on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- thank you, Mr. President. I don't know that that was specifically taken into account, but I don't think the anticipation was that he would fly on Wednesday afternoon, for example. So I can check. I don't think that made a difference in the calculation. I think the idea was that he could complete his testimony at any point on Wednesday if that's what the Court is inquiring about in terms of the schedule. But, as I indicated, our previous understanding was that both witnesses had commitments that required them to complete their testimony by Tuesday in whatever order, and then Mr. Djurdjevic had some additional flexibility which allowed for the possibility that we could conclude his testimony on Wednesday, but not later than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was mistaken. We are sitting in the morning on Wednesday. It is on Tuesday that we are sitting in the afternoon. Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. And I just wanted to underscore or perhaps slightly amplify another matter and a continuing concern of the Prosecution. Mr. Nicholls raised the 90(H) issue. Of course we understand that 90(H) provides for cross-examination that goes beyond the scope of the direct examination, which is a practical accommodation to the -- at least in large part, to the travel requirements of witnesses. However, as I discussed recently with Mr. Robinson, there's clearly a stretching point to that provision of 90(H) because what it amounts to is a direct examination by the Prosecution and a cross-examination by the Defence, then a lengthy and sometimes potentially lengthier than the Prosecution direct examination, a lengthy direct examination by the Defence without cross-examination by the Prosecution, without the provision for that. That's clearly not fair to the Prosecution, it's clearly not fair to the Court, and clearly not fair to the truth-seeking process. Mr. Robinson did not dispute that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. But it's difficult to deal with it in a vacuum. We'll deal with it when it arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand. But I think when a request is made for cross-examination for purposes of leading affirmative evidence of this length, we have encountered that very situation, and I think we have touched upon it previously. Prosecution has been willing to accommodate so as not to interrupt the schedule, but it clearly has an impact on our ability to respond. And on the time we take in re-direct examination it consumes -- that would -- that should normally be cross-examination time that doesn't cut into the time allotted for the presentation of our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could also -- I have to say in this particular instance I really agree with Mr. Tieger. The Prosecution called this witness in the Srebrenica component of its case and have about three or four relatively compact areas in which they want to -- in which they did examine him, but he's -- he was in his position throughout the whole war. We have ethnic cleansing, Sarajevo, hostages, all of those are topics that Dr. Karadzic wants to explore with this witness. And I think that the best solution and probably the fairest to the Prosecution and the witness and everybody given the timing is that Dr. Karadzic try to conclude what would normally be within the scope of the direct examination, and then at another time take up all these other issues. Because I think that Mr. Tieger is correct, and also from our side, measuring the length of his testimony by the length of the direct will really not allow us to have all the benefit of all the witness's evidence that we feel we need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. There's one further matter I need to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is what we are going to do. Thanks to the understanding and indulgence of interpreters and court reporters, we'll be sitting till 4.30 today after having a half an hour break at 3.00. And then on Monday, Mr. Karadzic, you will have about two hours, which means we should conclude this witness's evidence, including the re-examination, in two sessions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you should remain on relevant issues, relevant to the indictment. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I regret -- I'm sorry to have heard that General Simic is on his death-bed, but before I go on to this document I wanted to ask you whether you know whether General Simic was in any way -- or did he receive anything negative from me after this response, the tone of which is very strident? Was the relationship identical, was it a respectful relationship?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't even know of this response until today, but I know that General Simic, after this event, continued to have your photograph and his in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this please be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2156, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D03912.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you said that I visited you in the eastern part of Republika Srpska in Drvar, and you were at the forward command post there and you were involved in Bihac, or rather, the counter-offensive, the defence against the 5th Corps. Do you remember that on that occasion I took the decision according to which General Mladic should be the special advisor for the co-ordination of joint defence? This was a sort of replacement of a kind. Can you see this decree of mine that relates to this matter?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you spoke of just a moment ago happened on the 3rd of August, two days after the session of the Supreme Command. There was you and Krajisnik and Subotic and that chief of state security, his name escapes me now, Krnjajic. When you started speaking about this, I asked you whether all the attendees were welcome, and you sent away Krnjajic and you and Krajisnik stayed on. Everything you put to me now is correct. It is true that I refused to assume the duty of Chief of General Staff. Krajisnik's comment was the following: The general is a reasonable man. Tomorrow he's going to receive an order in writing and he probably will not refuse an order from the Supreme Command. And the next day this arrived, so you have it with the date of the 4th of September, or rather, the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D2157.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 10891.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mladic did not agree with this decree of mine, right, just like many others didn't? Can you take a look. This is the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska writing to the corps commands, and then the command of the East Bosnia Corps is citing in the first paragraph what the Main Staff did. Please read this if you haven't read it before. Read the -- at least the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there's no need for me to read it. I don't know when I read this, but it would be a good thing for me to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before your comment, just let us take a look at a few particular sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this sentence "organisational solutions." It's around the middle. It's the seventh line in the second paragraph: "Organisational solutions according to which the supreme commander directly commands the army do not exist in the theory and practice of armed struggle." Do you remember that that was the position of General Mladic stated in this letter sent to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was not only General Mladic's position. That is also a legal provision that we spoke about yesterday, and your advisors completely missed the point and they proclaimed you the supreme commander of the Army of Republika Srpska and automatically linked you to this, which Mladic is denying now. Although, as far as this document of Mladic's is concerned, I have quite a bit of criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The third paragraph from the top: "Proceeding from patriotic, human, and soldierly options, I cannot accept arbitrariness of the president of the RS, abuse of office, and anti-constitutional action." In other words, he refused my order.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mladic's position that it is completely contrary to the one taken on the previous day. He issued this document on the 5th, and we discussed this order of yours on the 4th, or rather, this decree of yours. On the 4th when Mladic read your decree to the generals, because he and I received them along parallel lines, this is what he said verbatim, "I think that Mane," that is my nickname, "can bring this to an end and I can withdraw." But in this sentence he is taking a position that is the total opposite: He does not want to withdraw. I found out about this letter late. I didn't know about it during the struggle - perhaps I can say that now - against you and against the Main Staff. I initiated the petition of the group of generals sent to the Assembly so that the Assembly could annul your decision, guided by the following: The Assembly appointed Mladic and they can relieve him of his duty. So this is something that I did not know about; namely, that Mladic at the collegium of the Main Staff asked us to accept his replacement; and here he addresses soldiers and subordinate commanders, asking them to protect him so that there would be no replacement. That was a great disappointment for me. If we can see this comment and the signature of General Novica Simic underneath Mladic's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a quotation and then Simic says that this should be forwarded.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please zoom in because I cannot read this, and I really am interested in this comment. I am surprised by this comment, too, because Simic, together with 21 of us -- there were 21 signatories of that petition that was addressed to you not to have Mladic replaced. And now he supports this letter of Mladic's? I mean, I don't know. All right. Never mind. Let us not deal with Simic now. I think that I've answered your question, namely, what I think about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted. And before the break I would just like to tender this petition that General Milovanovic, spoke about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2158, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 3.30. I thank, again, the staff for their understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A CLSS translation has come back for D2146, that was the 1st Krajina Corps document from 1 November 1992 that we saw earlier. So I think it doesn't need to be marked for identification. We have one available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And now I'm not sure whether it was yesterday or the day after yesterday, I forgot to mention that the CLSS would take a look into the translation of directive number 4, whether it's "together with" or "with." So I will ask CLSS to take a look into it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. As for interpretation, perhaps I could point out to the interpreters what it is that I was getting at in this sentence that was in dispute. Could we now please have 1D03901.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, you mentioned the petition that you initiated and we will have it before us in a moment and let's see who signed it. Is this that document, General? Do you recall? It's dated 5/6 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at the third paragraph, for instance: "In line with this, the Decision by the President of the RS relieving the Commander of the VRS ... was discussed and some other system, organisational and personnel changes in the VRS were discussed." So is this a reference to the transformation of the Main Staff to become a General Staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the fourth paragraph -- actually -- yes, the fourth paragraph said that people individually and unanimously expressed their view on this and then it says that no one consulted the -- that the VRS general could not accept or implement the decision in the preparation of which no one from the VRS was consulted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the signature page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mladic's name appears there but he didn't sign this but the other generals did; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you allow me, I'd like to explain how this petition came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mladic summoned the generals and when I said the sentence that he said then when -- in opening the statement and that he said that he was thinking of withdrawing and thinking that I could complete that job, his job, I protested immediately and I did not explain why it was that I did not want to accept this. And my explanation to him was not the same as the one that I gave you. I said to him, What fool would accept to command army which was in strategic retreat, and what fool would bear the responsibility for everything that had happened to us? Mladic agreed with my position, but then he asked me, What am I to do? I suggested that the generals of the VRS should refuse to implement this order of the Supreme Command, fully aware of the consequences that might ensue. And then he asked me how we were to carry that out, what was my idea. And I said that by nightfall I would summon all the generals to come to Banja Luka and present the problem to them, although ten of those generals were already there. So I told him that I would present the problem to them and ask them that we all sign a petition addressed to the National Assembly, with the demand that your decision on removing Mladic be annulled. The transformation of the Main Staff into a General Staff was not even mentioned then, although that, too, was a bad decision. Changing the essence of an institution such as the Main Staff in the final phases was not a good idea. He told me to do what I thought was best. We did what we did. I sent a telegram to all the generals. I prohibited General Miletic from coming, he was my deputy on the Main Staff, and General Galic who was in the midst of some operation on Majevica. I think 18 generals came, there were 18 of us. In the course of the afternoon, following my telegram, I received a telegram from the Supreme Command. I can't recall if you signed it to the effect that the generals were prohibited from going to Banja Luka. Now, out of all the generals who had been invited, only General Milosevic did not show up; he was the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. We explained to the men what the issue was, and as it says here "unanimously" and so on, all of that is as it was. All of these people signed the petition. Gvero and Tolimir were supposed to take this petition to the Assembly. General Galic met up with them in Zabare at the forward command post and signed the petition there. General Miletic awaited in Han Pijesak, I believe, and he, too, signed the petition. On the following day Milosevic reported to me and asked where he could sign the petition, and I asked him, Why didn't you do it last night? Why didn't you show up? And he said, Well, the supreme commander forbade -- he sent a telegram to that effect, he forbade me to go. So where could I go and sign this? However, Gvero did not let him sign it. So this is how this petition came into being. I learned of Mladic's paper much later, his address to the army where he is appealing with the subordinate commanders not to let him go. I was terribly disappointed. The day before he offered to resign from this post of commander of the Main Staff, or rather, commander of the army, and now, on the other hand, he was addressing the subordinates, asking their support for his remaining the commander of the army. So this is the background of this whole story with the petition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I hope that everyone noted that the first addressee is the National Assembly and the second addressee is the president of the republic. We can see that on the first page. If necessary, can we get back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you told that on that very day, on the 6th at the Assembly session, I criticise -- I criticised extensively some of the generals and I said that they weren't my officers. This was recorded in the minutes. Did anyone report it to you? That was my reaction to Milutinovic's and Gvero's interventions there. I was very sharp in my discussion on that -- at that Assembly session, and you probably received information thereof.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening or the next day, Gvero informed me that the Assembly had adopted our petition and annulled your decision. And, frankly speaking, I was happy because that meant I was off the hook. I wouldn't have to be tried before a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could we please pull up 1D05436 and just for your information, Gvero misinformed you. It was not -- my decision was not overturned. Actually, they were split, the votes were split. Dobrica Cosic and everybody else were calling for that decision to be rescinded.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that but I'm grateful because if it had come to me being tried I would have witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please take a look at this and would you agree with me that this is a communique, it's not a decision, it's a communique which I signed and said that, "Taking into consideration the appeal of his holiness the Patriarch Pavle," I did not mention the Serbian Assembly but it certainly was a very important element in this decision, but I inform that I decided to suspend the changes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the date, that was the 11th of August.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that. It's handwritten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall this, that this was my explanation?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this document. This is the first time that I see it. And this would have been in my favour still, well done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, were you aware that I publicly decided to suspend these changes, correct, and I wouldn't have been able to implement them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now have 1D05300.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll move to a new topic, General, the position of our army vis-a-vis the UNPROFOR. First of all, do we agree that under international law - and that's what was done - the UNPROFOR was in our country pursuant to our decision and it had a mandate that we accepted and that they could not have been in our country, on our territory, without our approval?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The presence of UNPROFOR on the territory of the SFRY was sought by the, I believe, already Rump Presidency of the SFRY in order to protect the Serbian people in Croatia. When the conflict broke out, at first inter-ethnic and later also inter-religious in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Federal Presidency decided, but I don't know at whose proposal, whether it was at the proposal of Alija Izetbegovic or yours, that UNPROFOR should also come to Bosnia and Herzegovina and it would have three mandates. I cannot give you the exact order of these three mandates, but I believe that I can name them. One of them, one of the missions was the escort of humanitarian aid convoys. The second mandate, I believe, was the role of observer in order to establish who was triggering a conflict or a particular operation and who engaged in disproportionate fire. And I can't recall the third. Can you help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe the third role was mediation and also the issues of water-supply, electric supply, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not what I meant. I will probably -- it will probably come to me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please take a look at this. Was this very early on - this is the 21st -- the 22nd of November, 1992, a document that you drafted, where you call for a civilised relationship of friendly relationship of our military personnel towards UNPROFOR. And in the first few paragraphs you explain why this was necessary. And then you order to corps commands what they were to -- what steps they were to take and so on. I can't recall everything. Can you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can I just see the signature, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a copy from the East Bosnia Corps, but I believe that all corps received this; correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A similar document was also sent by General Gvero. That's why I wanted to see the signature. He was the chief of the department for morale, guidance, religious, and political affairs. That's why I wanted to see whether the document that we have before us was issued by me or by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2 you can see that you ordered your staff to show a positive attitude towards UNPROFOR; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because at that time I believe that UNPROFOR was an objective representative of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2161, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have to skip a few things. I would like to call up 1D5313. This is a document which was issued in August 1993; again, one of your documents. Can we zoom in for the benefit of the General. On the 1st of August, 1993, this was issued to provide for the delivery of humanitarian aid, and then you issue an order. There are several bullet points, for example, the first, the second, the third, and the sixth are of some interest; the other ones are of a technical nature. Please look at the document and can you tell us in your own words what the order entailed? Under bullet point 3 you said the civilian authorities should inform the civilians of the position of the president of RS, the RS prime minister, and the VRS GS commander that the approved movement of UNPROFOR teams and humanitarian aid convoys must not be prevented or blocked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see that my position, the position of prime minister, and the position of the command of the Main Staff were identical in this matter; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and all those positions were in line with the spirit of what UNPROFOR requested and demanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at bullet point 6, where it says: "Familiarise yourself fully with the quality of personnel at all check-points, urgently remove all those who might provoke incidents or be profiteers and those who fail to respect the requests and orders of their superior officers." This was yet another way you used in order to secure an unhindered deployment of humanitarian aid; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I also wanted to represent the Army of Republika Srpska as an organised army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can we now go to the last page for the benefit of the General. And, again, under bullet point 5 you ask the civilian authorities to help the city of Sarajevo with the supply of electricity, gas, and so on and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D5304.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is another of your orders. Please pay attention to the date. It was issued on the 2nd of April, 1993, in the midst of the Podrinje crisis when large combat operations were going on in Podrinje; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, despite the fighting you issue an -- issued an order to corps commands and the commands of independent units to pay a lot of attention to the convoys of humanitarian organisations and UNPROFOR. I believe that in the examination-in-chief you made a distinction between UNPROFOR convoys that supplied UNPROFOR and those that they escorted and were organised by the organisations that provided humanitarian aid to the civilian population; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discovered through UNPROFOR convoys, not through the convoys organised by humanitarian organisations that UNPROFOR is involved in illegal dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that, General, sir, but now look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you ask a question about convoy, Mr. Nicholls, in your examination-in-chief? I don't think General did deal with the convoy issue at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Just at the beginning of my examination I asked him about the role of - if I get the name right - Milos Djurdjic and he explained that he was on the commission for humanitarian aid and that is related to the topic. But I didn't speak about convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, General, sir, that under bullet point 2 you assigned tasks to escorts and you assign patriots, educated people, professionally capable members of the VRS to be convoy escorts; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There are many other interesting things in here, but let's now display the last page of this document for the benefit of the General. He will see who the author of the document was and when it was dispatched. This is your document, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of June it was sent. I can't see the -- I can't see the month very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was on the 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was on the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's the 17th of June or the 17th of August. The two figures are very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 1 there is a different date, the 2nd of April. I don't know why there is a different date on the stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted? It's not very legible, is it? It must have been April; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the cover page -- page 1 says in typing "2nd of April," but this seems like 17th of June or August, as the General read out. But it's a matter for later assessment. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2163, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that this clock is showing a wrong time, 20 minutes later than it actually is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That shows some wishful time. We have about half an hour more for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted? And now I would like to call up 1D5301. I have only a translation on the screen and can we see the Serbian version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here, General, sir, it says in the English - this is also your document - that you issued on the 9th of April and you explain some details about inspection of humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR convoys, and you say that the Main Staff on the 8th of April -- or, I apologise, on the 2nd of April, dealt with the question of the movement of humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR convoys through the territory of Republika Srpska. Given the conduct and attitude of UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations and in order to take efficient measures, I hereby order, and then you go on to say -- I'd better read in English: [In English] "1. Perform an individual analysis of the quality of each member of the group for inspections of humanitarian aid convoys. Expel all from the group who have compromised themselves for personal profit or any other cause. "2. Appoint as leader of the working group an officer of proven honesty who is ethical and professionally capable." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. Can we now go on to the following page to show the signature and the date. It was sent on the 9th of April. This is also your document but it has been translated into English. You go on to say to reduce the possibility of the number of incidents happening by choosing the best people to those positions; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we can locate the B/C/S version of this later on. With that understanding, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to call up 1D5320.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, General, that our army, our people's army, comprised some people who were not exactly professional in their conduct. That's why you had to remove them and replace them by better people and that you sought the best people for this duty because it was to be expected that our people's army was not really a professional army; right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also one of your documents. It was issued on the 25th November, 1993. You sent it to all corps, and you say in this document: "Checks on humanitarian aid convoys. "Order." You say: "So far, there have been no serious problems with receiving, checking, and ensuring safe passage as a result of the professional conduct by those involved in this process." And then in the second paragraph you say: "Apart from this, there are still individual cases of unprofessional, improper, uncivilised and even arrogant behaviour leading to undesirable incidents ..." In the following paragraph in the last sentence, you say, "In order to eliminate the aforementioned defects, I order ...," and there follows a list of orders to amend the situation. Do you remember that document of yours?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this particular order. However, I remember many other similar orders. Wherever a problem appeared, I reinstated my previous orders. I reminded the existing commanders of their duty or I briefed those who had been appointed in the meantime, all with a view to raising their awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D2165.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D00275.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This will show us how I was very often unjust towards you and the Main Staff because foreigners thought that this -- that was a position of our entire army and not only of the individuals that you finally eliminated from the ranks of the army. Do you remember this, where it says my earlier order to quickly and without any stagnation made the requests of humanitarian organisations, had not been respected with regard to humanitarian issues. And then under number 3 it says: "The announcements for the public are too frequent and too long, thus they lose effectiveness." Do you agree and do you remember that I often showed suspicions about our own army based on the criticism of the foreigners who were involved in the process? And this was not -- that was not fair conduct on my behalf, the criticism was not justified.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The lack of fairness resulted from the fact that you accepted information from individuals without taking into account their ranks. Whoever told you something about the way the convoys were escorted, that was your reaction towards the Main Staff. Let me remind you of a situation when I attacked you, when I criticised you. That was on the 27th of March, 1994. And I asked you how you could strike an agreement with Yasushi Akashi about our artillery around Sarajevo to surrender to UNPROFOR. Mr. Koljevic was present and you were taken by surprise that I was privy to that information. And I had received that information on that same day in the morning at a meeting with General van Baal. He was the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR for Bosnia and Herzegovina. On that day I held a regular meeting with him -- that person -- that man simply wanted to cheat me, to -- in other words, I received information from somebody who was not competent to share that information with me. I was supposed to receive it from either you or from General Akashi. However, he was overly ambitious. He wanted to do something very strange. And this is what happened to you: Very often you received information from people who were not competent. For example, a driver from UNPROFOR who didn't like being stopped by anybody, and then he would tell you, We were ill treated by the Serbs, and then you criticised the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2166, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see 1D5311.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an order of yours and the date is ten days after this. But while waiting for it, General, do you know that Mr. van Baal testified here and stated that you told him that they shouldn't let trams through because you would order snipers to be active. In his notes that wasn't found and that was another disappointment concerning General van Baal. What do you say, did you ever order or did you ever tell him that you would order snipers to target trams?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a miserable army if it has a general such as General van Baal. We met on the 27th of March, 1994. And this had been ordered by Krajisnik, or rather, Krajisnik had organised this regular meeting of ours. The subject of the meeting was supposed to be the passage of humanitarian convoys. Once a month we would meet. The chiefs of staff from UNPROFOR would meet with me and we would analyse things and try and deal with the missions, and so on and so forth. On that morning at the meeting, I was attacked by van Baal. Similarly, General Ramsay did the same before him in relation to Markale. On the 26th, one day earlier, snipers opened fire on a tram in Marin Dvor. And first of all he asked me whether I knew about that. I said, No, that happened a day before, and the corps command probably didn't inform me of the fact. How did that happen? Well, he said, The Serbs opened fire on the tram. I said, Where was the tram? He said, In Marin Dvor. Marin Dvor was a centre for the Muslim part of Sarajevo. I said, General, how do you know they were Serbs? I wasn't claiming that they weren't, but, How do you know they were Serbs? Well, his answer was more or less, It can't be anyone else. I said, do you know how far Marin Dvor is from the VRS positions, what the maximum or minimum distance would be? He didn't know so I told him. The soldier who was closest to Marin Dvor was 5 and a half kilometres away. Which -- what kind of sniper can fire on targets 5 and a half kilometres away? You know, General, there were two shots that entered the tin above the entrance of the tram. So the tram was targeted from above. Later I found out that two women had been wounded; one of them was a Croat, the other was a Serbian. Neither was Muslim. I told him -- not just him. Whenever I met anyone from UNPROFOR, I asked them to influence the Muslim side since they had declared a state of war. You know what the procedure is in urban places. There's no public gathering because they complain that we were shelling them all the time, opening fire from all sorts of weapons. Secondly, football matches shouldn't organised, the theatres and cinemas shouldn't be opened, people shouldn't gather at squares, the lights are turned off at night. I said on that occasion, Well, please, influence the Muslims. So they put a stop to urban transport because people are concentrated here in a very small area. And in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, a country that has declared a state of war has to apply this procedure. He laughed cynically, and he asked me, Well, what will happen if we don't do this? And I said, I can't guarantee that some idiot won't open fire. When he testified in the Slobodan Milosevic case - I don't know whether it was in this courtroom or somewhere else, but it was in this building - I followed the proceedings and I can't put this in a different way. I'm a general and I say what I think I should say. General van Baal lied in front of the Tribunal. When I -- when he said I said, We'll open fire. Fortunately for me or for someone else, on one occasion, probably after the war at the time of the bombing of Yugoslavia, or rather, Serbia, in 1999, I told Milosevic about this, so he knew about it and he could refute what was said at the time. In your case, I don't know when he testified, I didn't follow that, but people told me that he made the same claim. On the 27th, when I attacked you for reaching an agreement according to which we were to surrender our artillery, have it withdrawn 20 kilometres from Sarajevo, well, you said that that wasn't the case, that we'd never spoken about that, and that you wouldn't have agreed to that without having consulted the Main Staff. Then I asked for your protection, if you remember. When you were at those meetings, those peace conferences, I asked you to try to influence the mediators and the warring parties, to make sure that there wouldn't be public gatherings so that we could reduce the losses sustained, the Muslim losses. They complained about losses; we didn't. A few days afterwards, a few days after that meeting at the beginning of April, van Baal called me to a meeting at the Corlic [phoen] sports airport in Cazinska Krajina. He wanted us to discuss the 5th Corps. I didn't ask for your approval or for the approval of Mladic either, but I quite simply didn't want to do that. He wanted to take me to Cazinska Krajina where Atif Dudakovic was in power so we could discuss Atif Dudakovic's corps. Furthermore, he would often call me. On one occasion, I said - and I think it's somewhere in the transcripts of my interviews -- he thought I was his secretary, or rather, he behaved as if I were his secretary. Every 15 to 20 minutes he would call me day and night. He needed something, he didn't understand something, but what was at stake? Well, in fact, when General Rose, his boss, left Bosnia and Herzegovina, he would call Alija Izetbegovic, he would call you - I don't know whether he called Mate Boban, whether he was alive at the time - and you'd dismiss him. He wasn't on your level and that was fine. And then he would call the commanders of the warring parties, Ratko Mladic, Rasim Delic, Milivoj Petkovic, and they would give him the cold shoulder, too. Then he would call me. He wanted a meeting, and so on and so forth. So he was trying to prove something about himself, about his capabilities, but he had no such capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Please, could you now have a look at your order here dated the 22nd of June, 1993. Say that some idiot apparently opened fire on UNPROFOR or I believed their report, and you are prohibiting anyone from opening fire; isn't that correct? Can we have a look at page 2 in the English version. Do you remember that you often prohibited such activity?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D2167.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we see 1D5372, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, please have a look at this. It's the command of the Drina Corps, Chief of Staff, I can't see the name, but have a look at this on the 30th of December, 1993, in the second paragraph -- in the first paragraph an attack on the area of Bljeceva from Srebrenica is mentioned. 1.400 people went out and launch an attack. In the second paragraph it says that UNPROFOR is abusing its convoys, bringing supplies to Muslims in Gorazde. The SNB has information that UNPROFOR members brought a large quantity of fuses for shells from Gorazde to Sarajevo on the 8th of December, 1993, and that written messages, money, packages, and similar are being transferred. Do you remember that we remained silent for a long time and we would look away when there were cases of abuse. We're not saying it was the command that was involved, but there was such cases that related to their vehicles and whether the command or individuals were responsible for these cases, well it's not that important. Does this reflect what you were aware of? Does this reflect the issue you had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I started explaining this and then you interrupted me. You said that there wasn't time to discuss the matter. The first legitimate activities relating to the delivery of assistance to the Muslim enclaves, we discovered this in UNPROFOR convoys, in fact, not in humanitarian organisations convoys. So this was done in the following manner: At the check-points -- or check-points would report to their superior commands, and then the corps commands would relay the information to us, to the Main Staff. In the part of the report on goods that were being transported, I noticed in several such reports, in fact, that a certain quantity of ammunitions for the needs of UNPROFOR was also being provided. And so on one occasion when a new UNPROFOR convoy was announced, I asked the UNPROFOR Chief of Staff who was in contact with me about the matter. I think it was General Ramsay. I asked him whether they were involved in military activity of any kind during the previous week, combat training, anything that would involve engaging the troops. And he said, No. So I said that, Last week you replenished your reserves of ammunition and your reserves of fuel, but you did not use them. So why are these things being delivered in the convoys again? Why is ammunition and fuel being transported in these convoys again? I don't know what his answer was. It didn't make much sense. It was something to the fact that they were planning to do something and had to replenish these supplies. But I came to the conclusion, although I couldn't prove it, that they were providing weapons and ammunition to the Muslims. I said this to General Rose, and he was surprised. He said it was impossible. Later we found reservoirs with dual containers in UNPROFOR vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll now refer to a protest that you lodged --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But could this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No -- I'm not objecting to a document. Just for the incident -- and I'm sorry to interrupt. The incident which the witness has just described, this particular convoy and the conversation he had with General Rose, I just wonder for our record when this was and where the convoy was going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, General, could you help us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The convoy was entering Gorazde. I can't remember the exact time, but this soon became a mass phenomenon. And particular humanitarian organisations, in particular UNHCR, started acting the same way as UNPROFOR convoys. This concerns these three Eastern Bosnian enclaves at least. I think that the date is not that important. What is important is that after the report from UNPROFOR, after those mixed commissions that we have discussed today on disarming Muslim troops in the enclaves, so it was from May 1993 up until January 1994, the number of Muslim troops in those enclaves in January 1994 was about 16.500, and these troops were armed and they were part of the 28th Division whose command was in the centre of Srebrenica. Two brigades were in Srebrenica. One of those -- that division's brigades was in Zepa. The 81st Division with its HQ in Gorazde was established. After the Operation Zvijezda 94, it remained there. That was when the Gorazde safe haven had been reduced to a circle, the diameter which was 3 kilometres. No one can convince me of the fact that UNPROFOR wasn't familiar with the existence of that army. No one can convince me that UNPROFOR did not organise the delivery of weapons and ammunition to the Muslims in those enclaves. The parachute operation delivering supplies to enclaves from the air was no more than a smoke-screen that UNPROFOR created to conceal the delivery of weapons. Sometimes these deliveries ended up on the Serbian side and our troops could hardly wait for a parachute to land on their side. They expected to find food and other such things, but in one package they found ammunition for a 12.7-millimetre machine-gun. It was in these flour packages. The soldier who found it saw that the packages were very heavy, that's how he discovered it. One such package was sent to the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo as proof that weapons and ammunition were being delivered to the enclaves. We never heard about the results of the investigation, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as Exhibit D2168. We'll call for the day here today. General, we'll continue on Monday morning at 9.00. I hope we will be able to conclude your evidence during the course of the morning on that day. The hearing is adjourned.
